Chapter 2 Stress and equilibrium

2.9 Turned axes

Of the two questions still open, we now take up the first one, how the stress components change when we turn the axes. The second, on which face through the point the normal stress is largest, will wait for section 2.11.

The stress components at a point \(P\) are the components of three traction vectors on the faces through \(P\) that are perpendicular to the axes of the coordinate system, split along these axes. If we turn the axes, these are three other faces, other traction vectors act on them, and we split each of them along other axes. How do we compute the nine numbers in the new axes from the nine numbers in the old ones?

The question is not only one of computation. In the bar of section 2.4 only a normal stress acted on the cross section, but on an oblique cut there was also a shear stress, and for steel it is the shear stress that approximately decides when yielding begins (BOWER §3.7.3, PDF p. 146). In the pure shear of section 2.6.6 only shear stresses acted on the faces of the cube, but on the diagonal faces only tension and compression. In a plate reinforced with fibres we want the stress on faces along the fibres and across them, not on faces along the edges of the plate (CM Example 4.3.1, PDF p. 186). We place the axes where the computation is easiest, but we need the stress on faces that the material and the structure choose.

The goal of this section is the rule that gives the components in one rectangular Cartesian coordinate system from the components in another. We will derive it first for vectors, then for stress and for strain. Stress and strain will turn out to have the same rule, and this very rule will say exactly what the word means with which books name such quantities. Along the way we will write Cauchy's formula with matrices and show how the shear strain measures the change of a right angle, which in chapter 1 we derived only to first order, with the tangents of the tilts of the fibres.

What do we assume? Both coordinate systems are rectangular Cartesian, with the same unit of length, and their origins are at the same point. The last is no restriction. The components of a vector are differences of coordinates ((1.8)), and if we move the origin without turning the axes, the coordinates of all points change by the same three numbers, while their differences stay. We assume nothing about the body or the material. What we derive for stress holds at every interior point at which Cauchy's formula holds (theorem 2.26 and its extension to a moving body after it). From section 2.3 we will use the fact that the length of a vector and the scalar product of two vectors are the same numbers in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with the same unit. The symmetry of the stress components (theorem 2.41) we will need only for the simplified formulas ((2.54), the expanded \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) and (2.60)), while the rule (2.59) does not need it. For strain we assume, as in section 1.17, a continuously differentiable displacement field (definition 1.91) and small partial derivatives of the displacements.

2.9.1 The rotation matrix

In section 1.5.5 we turned the axes by a quarter turn about the axis \(z\) and found that the flight of the fly, which had the components \((1, 2, -2)\) in the old axes, has the components \((2, -1, -2)\) in the new axes. We got there by thinking about how many steps along which new axis make up the flight. For an arbitrary turn such thinking is no longer simple, so we need a rule.

From history

The question of how to get the coordinates of a point in one rectangular system from its coordinates in another system with the same origin is older than matrices. MUIR counts it among the problems of coordinate geometry (MUIR, PDF p. 433). As the first paper on his list of papers about it he gives Euler's book Introductio in analysin infinitorum of 1748, more precisely its appendix on surfaces (MUIR, PDF p. 433). The list also contains papers on the rotation of a body, among them Lagrange's of 1773 (MUIR, PDF p. 434). In a rotating body the axes attached to it turn relative to the axes at rest, and this is exactly our problem. Expressions in the coefficients of equations, which we shall meet in section 2.10, appeared in attempts to solve this problem only comparatively late. Probably this is because a change of coordinates does not reduce to mere elimination of unknowns from a system of linear equations (MUIR, PDF p. 433).

Let us return to the search for the rule that gives, from the components of a vector in the old axes, the components in the turned axes. We name the new axes \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) and \(\bar z\) and their unit vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\), as in section 1.5.5. The new axes, too, are the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system: they are mutually perpendicular, and lengths on them are measured with the same unit as on the old ones. So \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) are three unit vectors that are pairwise perpendicular. We can write each of them with components in the old system, like any other vector. For the quarter turn they are

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 0, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1) .\]

For a turn about the axis \(z\) by another angle, measured from the old axis \(x\) toward the old axis \(y\), let us take \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\), where \(c\) and \(s\) are numbers with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), so that the vector is a unit vector. For \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) we take \((-s, c, 0)\). This vector is a unit vector too, because \(s^2 + c^2 = 1\), and it is perpendicular to \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), because \(c\,(-s) + s\,c + 0 \cdot 0 = 0\). The axis \(z\) stays as it is, \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\), and this vector is perpendicular to both previous ones, because their component \(z\) is zero. The old unit vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) point along the old axes from the common origin \(O\). With \(c = 0\) and \(s = 1\) we get the quarter turn from above. We have met both vectors before. In section 2.4, \(\vek n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) was the unit normal of the oblique cut of the bar and \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\) the direction in the cut. So the numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are the cosine and the sine of the angle \(\theta\) by which the new axis \(x\) is turned from the old one toward the axis \(y\) (figure 2.108). We will not need the angle itself, the numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are enough. In the examples we take \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). This corresponds to the angle \(\theta = 53{,}13^\circ\).

We collect the nine components of the new unit vectors in a matrix, one vector in each row.

Definition 2.44 Rotation matrix (matrika zasuka)

Let two rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with the same unit of length be given, an old system with the unit vectors of the axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and a new system with the unit vectors of the axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\). The rotation matrix (matrika zasuka) is the \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat Q\) whose row \(k\) holds the components of the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the old system:

\[Q_{\mathrm{kj}} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} , \tag{2.50}\]

where the indices \(k\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The numbers \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) are the direction cosines (smerni kosinusi) of the new axes with respect to the old ones.

Source: CM (2.2.71), (2.2.72) (PDF pp. 58-59), where the matrix is written \([L]\) with the entries \(\ell_{\mathrm{ij}}\), SADD (1.4.1) (PDF p. 16), where it is written \(Q_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

What do these numbers mean? The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is the component \(j\) of the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) in the old system. By section 2.3 the component of a vector along the old axis \(j\) is its projection onto \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), as (2.50) says. For the angle \(\varphi\) between nonzero vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\), \(\cos\varphi = \vek a\cdot\vek b/(|\vek a|\,|\vek b|)\) (KREYSZIG §9.2 (4), PDF p. 388, section 2.3). The vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) are unit vectors, so their scalar product is the cosine of the angle between the new axis \(k\) and the old axis \(j\). Hence the name direction cosines. For the turn about the axis \(z\),

\[\mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} c & s & 0 \\ -s & c & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \text{and for } c = 0{,}6 \text{ and } s = 0{,}8 \qquad \mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & 0{,}8 & 0 \\ -0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = c = \cos\theta\) is the cosine of the angle \(\theta\) between the axes \(\bar x\) and \(x\). The entry \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = s = \sin\theta\) is the cosine of the angle \(90^\circ - \theta\) between the axes \(\bar x\) and \(y\), since \(\cos(90^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta\) (school trigonometry, as in section 2.4). CM writes the same matrix for plates with fibres turned by the angle \(\theta\) (CM (4.3.5), PDF p. 187).

Why the name rotation? We usually get the new system by turning the old one. The definition, however, also covers a new system in which the opposite positive direction is chosen on some axis, as in item 2 of the proof of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26). With the axis \(x\) reversed, for example, \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (-1, 0, 0)\). Such a system is not only turned but also mirrored. Everything we derive holds in both cases. CM keeps the name rotation (zasuk) for the case without mirroring (CM §2.3.7, PDF p. 68), and in section 2.10 we will see how the two cases are told apart by a single number.

How do we get the components of a vector in the new axes? The component of a vector along an axis is its projection onto the unit vector of that axis. So the new component \(\bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the scalar product \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\). The scalar product, however, has the same value in every rectangular Cartesian system, so we may compute it with the components in the old system, which we know. This is the whole idea of the next lemma.

Lemma 2.45 Components of a vector in turned axes (komponente vektorja v zasukanih oseh)

Let two rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with the same unit of length be given, and let \(\mat Q\) be the rotation matrix from the old one to the new one. Let a vector \(\vek a\) have the components \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the old system and \(\bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the new one. Then:

  1. \(\bar a_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(= \) \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\) for \(k = x, y, z\), in short
    \[\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q\,\vek a , \tag{2.51}\]
  2. \(a_{\mathrm{j}}\) \(= \) \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,\bar a_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(j = x, y, z\), in short \(\vek a = \mat Q^\T\,\bar{\vek a}\).

Here \(\vek a\) and \(\bar{\vek a}\) mean the columns of components of the same vector in the old and in the new system, and the sums run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that every new component is the sum of item 1 and every old component the sum of item 2. Both times we compute the same scalar product in two systems.

  1. In the new system the unit vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the components \((1, 0, 0)\) (definition 1.20, applied in the new system). By (2.6), computed in the new system, \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 1 + \bar a_{\mathrm{y}} \cdot 0 + \bar a_{\mathrm{z}} \cdot 0 = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. The scalar product has the same value in every rectangular Cartesian system with the same unit, because the formula \(\vek a\cdot\vek b = \tfrac12\left(|\vek a|^2 + |\vek b|^2 - |\vek b - \vek a|^2\right)\) of section 2.3 expresses it by lengths only. So we may also compute the number \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the components in the old system.
  3. In the old system \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\), and by definition 2.44 of the rotation matrix \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = (Q_{\mathrm{kx}}, Q_{\mathrm{ky}}, Q_{\mathrm{kz}})\). By (2.6), \(\vek a\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\,a_{\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{ky}}\,a_{\mathrm{y}} + Q_{\mathrm{kz}}\,a_{\mathrm{z}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\). Together with step 1 this is item 1.
  4. By (1.39) the three equations for \(k = x, y, z\) are the three components of the product \(\mat Q\,\vek a\) (definition 1.97). This is (2.51).
  5. For item 2 we swap the roles of the systems. By steps 1 and 2, applied to the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), the old unit vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) has in the new system the components \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\). The scalar product is symmetric (lemma 2.12, item 1), so these are the numbers \(Q_{\mathrm{xj}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yj}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{zj}}\), the column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\).
  6. As in steps 1 to 3, only with the systems swapped, \(a_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek a\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), and when we compute this scalar product with the components in the new system we get \(a_{\mathrm{j}} = \bar a_{\mathrm{x}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}} + \bar a_{\mathrm{y}}\,Q_{\mathrm{yj}} + \bar a_{\mathrm{z}}\,Q_{\mathrm{zj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,\bar a_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  7. By definition 1.101 of the transposed matrix, the number \(Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is the entry in row \(j\) and column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat Q^\T\), so by (1.39) the sum of step 6 is the component \(j\) of the product \(\mat Q^\T\bar{\vek a}\).

Source: CM (2.2.70) (PDF p. 58), SADD (1.4.6), (1.4.7) (PDF p. 17). The sources derive the rule from writing the unit vectors of one system with the unit vectors of the other. The proof with the scalar product is not from the sources.

The proof showed that every new component is the projection onto a new unit vector, computed with the old components. Let us test the lemma on the flight of the fly \(\vek a = (1, 2, -2)\). For the quarter turn, by (1.39),

\[\mat Q\,\vek a = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot (-2) \\ (-1) \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot (-2) \\ 0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

which is what we found in section 1.5.5 by thinking. For the turn with \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\),

\[\bar a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}6 \cdot 1 + 0{,}8 \cdot 2 = 2{,}2 , \qquad \bar a_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}8 \cdot 1 + 0{,}6 \cdot 2 = 0{,}4 , \qquad \bar a_{\mathrm{z}} = -2 ,\]

so in the new axes the flight has the components \((\tfrac{11}{5}, \tfrac25, -2)\) (figure 2.109). Its length is \(\sqrt{2{,}2^2 + 0{,}4^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{4{,}84 + 0{,}16 + 4} = \sqrt 9 = 3\) m, the same as in the old axes, since the arrow is the same. Item 2 gives back the old components: \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}6 \cdot 2{,}2 - 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}4 = 1{,}32 - 0{,}32 = 1\) and \(a_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}2 + 0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}4 = 1{,}76 + 0{,}24 = 2\). In the figure on the left the flight vector, the arrow from the point \(O\), is composed of the step \(1\) along \(x\) and the steps \(2\) along \(y\) in the old axes. On the right is the same arrow from the same point \(O\), the old axes are grey, the new axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) blue, and the flight is composed of \(\tfrac{11}{5}\) steps along \(\bar x\) and \(\tfrac25\) steps along \(\bar y\).

The lemma holds only between rectangular Cartesian systems, where a component is the projection onto the unit vector of the axis. For the oblique axes of section 1.5.1 the components are not projections, and the rule is different (CM §2.2.4, PDF pp. 48-52).

The rule for the way back has the transposed matrix. When we translate components into the new system and then back, we must get the original ones, so we expect \(\mat Q^\T\) to be the inverse matrix of \(\mat Q\). Matrices with this property have a name.

Definition 2.46 Orthogonal matrix (ortogonalna matrika)

A square matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal (ortogonalna) if

\[\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = \mat I . \tag{2.52}\]

Source: CM (2.3.15) (PDF p. 68), SADD (1.4.9), (1.4.10) (PDF p. 17).

A square matrix is a matrix with as many rows as columns, and the definition holds for every size. By definition 1.110 of the inverse matrix, equation (2.52) says that the transposed matrix is the inverse, \(\mat Q^{-1} = \mat Q^\T\). The name says what the equation means for the rows. The entry in row \(k\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\), the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the rows \(k\) and \(l\), and the equation requires this sum to be \(1\) for \(k = l\) and \(0\) for \(k \neq l\). So the rows are pairwise perpendicular in the sense of definition 2.11, orthogonal, and each has length \(1\). The equation \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) says the same for the columns.

From history

The names orthogonal transformation (ortogonalna preobrazba) and orthogonal substitution (ortogonalna zamenjava) for the passage to new variables with such a matrix go back to 1852, both in the papers of Sylvester (MUIR, PDF p. 842).

The rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) of this section is orthogonal, as the following lemma says.

Lemma 2.47 Orthogonality of the rotation matrix (ortogonalnost matrike zasuka)

The rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal. Its rows are the components of the new unit vectors of the axes in the old system, and its columns are the components of the old unit vectors of the axes in the new system.

Proof

We must show both equalities in (2.52). We write every entry of the product as the scalar product of two unit vectors.

  1. By definitions 1.99 and 1.101 the entry \((k, l)\) of the product \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,(\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{jl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  2. By definition 2.44 the rows \(k\) and \(l\) are the components of the vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\) in the old system, so by (2.6) the sum of step 1 equals \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  3. The new unit vectors are unit vectors and pairwise perpendicular. So \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}} = |\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}|^2 = 1\) (lemma 2.12, item 4) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = 0\) for \(k \neq l\) (definition 2.11). These are exactly the entries of the identity matrix (definition 1.108), so \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = \mat I\).
  4. By step 5 of the proof of lemma 2.45 on the components of a vector in turned axes, the column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) is the triple of components of the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the new system.
  5. The entry \((i, j)\) of the product \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,Q_{\mathrm{kj}}\), the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the columns \(i\) and \(j\). By step 4 and by (2.6), computed in the new system, this is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  6. The old unit vectors are unit vectors and pairwise perpendicular as well, so, as in step 3, \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\).

Source: SADD (1.4.9), (1.4.10) (PDF p. 17), CM (2.5.20) (PDF p. 87). SADD derives the equalities from the two rules for components. The proof with the scalar products of rows and columns is not from the sources.

Let us test it for \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\). The sum of the squares of the entries of the first row is \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 + 0 = 1\), and the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the first and the second row is \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 \cdot 0 = 0\). The lemma also tells why the rule for the way back has the transposed matrix: item 2 of lemma 2.45 is \(\vek a = \mat Q^\T\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q^{-1}\bar{\vek a}\), the rule that undoes the rule of item 1.

The test must also be able to reject a matrix. In the same matrix we change a single sign: we replace the element \(-0{,}8\) in the second row by \(0{,}8\). We get the matrix \(\mat Q'\) with rows \((0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\), \((0{,}8;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\) and \((0;\ 0;\ 1)\). The matrix \(\mat Q'\) is not orthogonal if for some pair of rows \(k \neq l\) the sum of products of corresponding elements is not \(0\) or if some row has a length different from \(1\).

  1. The first row has the sum of squares \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 + 0 = 1\), the second \(0{,}64 + 0{,}36 + 0 = 1\), the third \(0 + 0 + 1 = 1\). Every row has length \(1\), since the sign of a square does not change.
  2. The sum of products of corresponding elements of the first and second rows is \(0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}8 + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 \cdot 0 = 0{,}48 + 0{,}48 = 0{,}96\). Before, the products \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8)\) and \(0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6\) subtracted, now they add.
  3. The number \(0{,}96\) is not zero, so the element \((1, 2)\) of the matrix \(\mat Q'\mat Q'^\T\) equals \(0{,}96\) and not \(0\). The matrix \(\mat Q'\mat Q'^\T\) has ones on the diagonal and \(0{,}96\) at the places \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 1)\), so it is not the identity matrix.
  4. Columns \(1\) and \(2\) of the matrix \(\mat Q'\) are \((0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\) and \((0{,}8;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\), and their sum of products is again \(0{,}96\), so also \(\mat Q'^\T\mat Q' \neq \mat I\).

The rows of the matrix \(\mat Q'\) are therefore not perpendicular, although they are unit vectors. In figure 2.110 the rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are drawn as arrows from \(O\) that make a right angle, and the products \(-0{,}48\) and \(0{,}48\) cancel. The rows of the matrix \(\mat Q'\) instead make an angle with cosine \(0{,}96\), a little more than \(16^\circ\), not \(90^\circ\).

The converse holds too. If \(\mat Q\) is any orthogonal \(3 \times 3\) matrix, then by what we just said its rows are three pairwise perpendicular unit vectors. Drawn from the origin, they determine three perpendicular axes with the same unit of length, that is, a new rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and \(\mat Q\) is its rotation matrix.

2.9.2 Cauchy's formula with matrices

At the end of section 2.6.5 we wrote the nine stress components in a table in which each row is one traction vector. In section 2.8.8 we already read this table as a matrix (definition 1.94) and saw that it is symmetric. Now we use it to write Cauchy's formula as the product of a matrix and a vector.

Definition 2.48 Stress matrix (matrika napetosti)

The stress matrix (matrika napetosti) \(\ten\sigma\) at a point \(P\) is the matrix of the stress components at \(P\) in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, in which row \(i\) holds the components of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\):

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{2.53}\]

Source: SADD (3.2.3) (PDF p. 65), BOWER §2.2.3 (PDF pp. 70-71). CM (4.2.11) (PDF p. 183) writes the transposed matrix.

The stress matrix is a record of the stress at a point in a chosen coordinate system, just as the triple of components is a record of a vector. When we turn the axes, the matrix changes, but the stress at the point stays the same. How the matrix changes we will derive in section 2.9.4. First let us write Cauchy's formula.

  1. By (2.27) the component \(x\) of the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). The numbers \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) are the column \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\).
  2. By definition 1.101 of the transposed matrix, the column \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) is the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma^\T\). So by (1.39) the sum of step 1 is the component \(x\) of the product \(\ten\sigma^\T\vek n\).
  3. The same holds for the components \(y\) and \(z\), so
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma^\T\vek n , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} t_{\mathrm{x}} \\ t_{\mathrm{y}} \\ t_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} n_{\mathrm{x}} \\ n_{\mathrm{y}} \\ n_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} .\]
  4. By theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\). So the stress matrix is symmetric (definition 1.103), \(\ten\sigma^\T = \ten\sigma\), and
    \[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n . \tag{2.54}\]

We used the symmetry only in step 4, where we equated \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). The formula \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma^\T\vek n\) holds without it too. CM writes \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\cdot\hat{\vek n}\) and in matrix form \(\{t\} = [\sigma]\{n\}\) (CM (4.2.10), (4.2.11), PDF p. 183), because its stress matrix is our matrix \(\ten\sigma^\T\). BOWER, who writes the indices as we do, writes \(\vek t(\vek n) = \vek n\cdot\ten\sigma\) and warns that because of the symmetry there is no difference between the two conventions (BOWER, PDF pp. 70-71). The difference becomes important for measures of stress that are not symmetric. We will meet them in section 2.13.

From the matrix form we also get the normal and the shear stress on a face with the unit normal \(\vek n\). By definition 2.18 the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n\). The component \(i\) of the vector \(\ten\sigma\vek n\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\), and exactly this double sum is the product of the row \(\vek n^\T\), the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) and the column \(\vek n\) ((1.42)). By item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, the shear stress is given by \(\tau^2 = |\vek t|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). Together:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek n^\T\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \tau^2 = |\ten\sigma\,\vek n|^2 - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}^2 . \tag{2.55}\]

The double sum has nine terms. The terms \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) are equal because of the symmetry, and the same holds for the other two pairs, so written out

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

This is how CM (4.2.17) writes the normal stress and CM (4.2.18) the shear stress (PDF p. 184).

The formula for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\) has the same form as the strain of a fibre in the direction \(\vek n\) in (1.61), only with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) instead of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The reason is that both quantities are built in the same way: a matrix maps the direction \(\vek n\) to a vector, and we project this vector back onto the direction \(\vek n\). For stress this vector is the force per unit area \(\ten\sigma\vek n\). For strain it is \(\mat H\vek n\), approximately the difference of the displacements of the ends of a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\), divided by its length (section 1.17). Its projection onto the direction of the fibre is \(\vek n^\T\mat H\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), because in the double sum the terms \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{j}}\,H_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\) combine into \(2\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Let us test the formulas on the pure shear of section 2.6.6. The cube is loaded only by forces along its faces. We label the vertices \(A\) bottom left, \(B\) bottom right, \(C\) top right and \(D\) top left. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(z\) up, we pull the top face to the right, the bottom one to the left, the right one up and the left one down, all with the same force per unit area \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa. The only nonzero stress components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). Take the face with the normal \(\vek n = (\tfrac35, 0, \tfrac45)\), which is perpendicular to neither diagonal of the cube. It cuts off a triangular piece, on whose bottom and left faces the shear force \(\tau_0\) per unit area acts (figure 2.111). By (2.54),

\[\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \tau_0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \tau_0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3/5 \\ 0 \\ 4/5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac45\,\tau_0 \\ 0 \\ \tfrac35\,\tau_0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 40 \\ 0 \\ 30 \end{bmatrix} \text{MPa} .\]

By (2.55) the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 2 \cdot 50 \cdot \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac45 = 48\) MPa, which is also \(\vek t\cdot\vek n = 40 \cdot \tfrac35 + 30 \cdot \tfrac45 = 24 + 24 = 48\) MPa. The traction vector has the size \(|\vek t| = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50\) MPa, and the shear stress is \(\tau = \sqrt{50^2 - 48^2} = \sqrt{196} = 14\) MPa. The shear part is \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = 14\ \text{MPa} \cdot (\tfrac45, 0, -\tfrac35)\), and it is indeed perpendicular to \(\vek n\), since \(\tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac35 + 0 \cdot 0 - \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac45 = 0\). On the face perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\), with the normal \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 0, 1)\), the normal stress was \(50\) MPa and there was no shear stress (section 2.6.6). The normal of our face is close to that normal, so the normal stress is only \(4\,\%\) below \(50\) MPa, while the shear stress is already \(28\,\%\) of \(\tau_0\), because it grows with the sine of twice the tilt \((2 \cdot 8{,}13^\circ = 16{,}26^\circ)\), while the normal stress falls with the cosine of the same angle. Why so different? For a small angle the sine is nearly the angle itself in radians, \(0{,}28\), while the cosine differs from 1 only by half the square of the angle, \(0{,}28^2/2 = 0{,}04\). A small tilt therefore brings shear at once and leaves the normal stress nearly as it was.

2.9.3 The normal of a curved surface and the gradient

All the faces on which we have computed the traction vector so far were flat. The surface of a shaft, a pipe or a ball is curved, though, and it is often across such a surface that a force is passed on, for example from a wheel to a shaft. In section 2.5.1 we defined the normal of a curved surface through the tangent plane. What stayed open is how to compute it from the equation of the surface. There are two questions: what the normal at a point is for a general set of points, and how we compute it from the equation of the surface.

Take a shaft of radius 5 cm whose axis is the axis \(z\). In figure 2.112, left, we look at it along the axis. The axes \(x\) and \(y\) start at the centre \(O\), and we measure lengths in centimetres. A point \((x, y, z)\) lies on the surface of the shaft exactly when it is 5 cm away from the axis \(z\), that is, when \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\). We move all the terms to the left side and call it

\[f(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 - 25 .\]

The function \(f\) takes the three coordinates of a point and gives one number. The surface of the shaft is the set of points where \(f = 0\). Inside the shaft \(f < 0\), outside it \(f > 0\). The points with \(f = -9\) are 4 cm away from the axis, since \(16 - 25 = -9\), and the points with \(f = 11\) are 6 cm away, since \(36 - 25 = 11\). These are the dashed circles. Every value of \(f\) greater than \(-25\) gives its own cylinder around the same axis. We know the same idea from a hiking map: a contour line joins the points with the same height above sea level, and whoever walks along it does not climb. Here a surface joins the points with the same value of the function \(f\).

Definition 2.49 Level surface (nivojska ploskev)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables and \(c\) a number. The level surface (nivojska ploskev) of the function \(f\) at the value \(c\) is the set of all points \((x, y, z)\) at which \(f\) is defined and \(f(x, y, z) = c\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.7 (PDF p. 424).

Level means a height, as with the circles in the figure, which correspond to the contour lines of a map. The name surface is given in advance, although the set is not always a surface: for our function it is only the axis \(z\) at \(c = -25\), and at \(c < -25\) it has no point at all.

How does \(f\) change when we move from a point by a short step? Take the point \(P = (3, 4, 2)\) on the surface of the shaft, \(f(P) = 9 + 16 - 25 = 0\), and a step to the point \(Q = (3 + \Delta x,\ 4 + \Delta y,\ 2 + \Delta z)\). By theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step,

\[f(Q) - f(P) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R(Q) ,\]

where the remainder \(R(Q)\) is small compared with the length of the step when the step is short. By (2.6) the first three terms are the scalar product of the step \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) with the triple of partial derivatives. So this triple acts as one vector, drawn from the point \(P\), and it gets a name.

Definition 2.50 Gradient of a function (gradient funkcije)

Let the function of three variables \(f\), written with the coordinates of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, have all three partial derivatives at the point \(P\) (definition 1.26). The gradient (gradient) of the function \(f\) at the point \(P\) is the vector

\[\nabla f(P) = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P),\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P),\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P)\Big) . \tag{2.56}\]

Source: KREYSZIG §9.7, definition 1 and (1) (PDF p. 422). The source notes that in curvilinear coordinates the gradient is written differently (PDF p. 422).

We read the sign \(\nabla\) as nabla. The components of the gradient are the slopes of the function \(f\) along the three axes, and the word gradient also means the slope of a road. For the shaft \(\partial f/\partial x = 2x\), \(\partial f/\partial y = 2y\) and \(\partial f/\partial z = 0\), because in the partial derivative with respect to one coordinate we hold the other two fixed. At the point \(P\), therefore,

\[\nabla f(P) = (2 \cdot 3,\ 2 \cdot 4,\ 0) = (6, 8, 0) , \qquad |\nabla f(P)| = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10 .\]

This is the blue arrow from the point \(P\), which points straight away from the axis of the shaft. It is drawn shorter than it is, because at the scale of the figure it would reach 5 cm far. Since \(f\) has the unit cm² and the step has cm, the components of the gradient have the unit cm.

Let us test what the gradient tells on two steps of length 1 cm from the point \(P\). The first goes in the direction of the gradient, the second perpendicular to it:

  • The step \((0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\) to the point \(N = (3{,}6;\ 4{,}8;\ 2)\). The scalar product with the gradient is \(6 \cdot 0{,}6 + 8 \cdot 0{,}8 = 10\). In fact \(f(N) = 12{,}96 + 23{,}04 - 25 = 11\), the point \(N\) lies on the circle \(f = 11\). The remainder is \(R = 11 - 10 = 1\).
  • The step \((-0{,}8;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\) to the point \(D = (2{,}2;\ 4{,}6;\ 2)\). The scalar product with the gradient is \(6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 8 \cdot 0{,}6 = 0\). In fact \(f(D) = 4{,}84 + 21{,}16 - 25 = 1\), the point \(D\) lies right next to the surface of the shaft. The remainder is again \(R = 1\).

In the direction of the gradient \(f\) changed by 11, perpendicular to it only by the remainder 1. Here we can compute the remainder exactly. When we multiply out the expression \((3 + \Delta x)^2 + (4 + \Delta y)^2 - 25\), we get \(6\,\Delta x + 8\,\Delta y + \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2\), so \(R = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2\), the square of the part of the step that is perpendicular to the axis of the shaft. For a step ten times shorter, 1 mm, the remainder is a hundred times smaller, \(0{,}01\), while the change in the direction of the gradient is only ten times smaller, \(1\). This is the whole idea of this section. Along the surface \(f\) does not change at all, and for a short step that is possible only if the step is nearly perpendicular to the gradient. So the gradient points perpendicular to the surface.

But what does perpendicular to a surface mean when the surface is curved? By definition 2.17 the unit normal of a flat face is perpendicular to every vector between two points of the face. On a curved surface there is no such vector. In figure 2.112, top right, the arc of the surface of the shaft near the point \(P\) is enlarged, with the unit vector \(\vek n = (0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\) in the direction of the gradient. From \(P\) we draw chords to three points of the surface, and for each we compute the scalar product \(\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}\) and the quotient \(\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}/|PQ|\). The quotient is the cosine of the angle between \(\vek n\) and the chord (section 2.3):

  • \(Q_1 = (0;\ 5;\ 2)\): the chord \((-3;\ 1;\ 0)\) of length \(3{,}162\), scalar product \(-1{,}8 + 0{,}8 = -1{,}00\), quotient \(-0{,}316\), angle \(108{,}4^\circ\).
  • \(Q_2 = (1{,}4;\ 4{,}8;\ 2)\): the chord \((-1{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\) of length \(1{,}789\), scalar product \(-0{,}96 + 0{,}64 = -0{,}32\), quotient \(-0{,}179\), angle \(100{,}3^\circ\).
  • \(Q_3 = (\tfrac{40}{17};\ \tfrac{75}{17};\ 2)\): a chord of length \(0{,}767\), scalar product \(-0{,}059\), quotient \(-0{,}077\), angle \(94{,}4^\circ\).

No chord is perpendicular to \(\vek n\). But the shorter it is, the closer it is to a right angle, and the better it fits the tangent, the line through \(P\) that is perpendicular to \(\vek n\). This is exactly what we ask of a normal: the quotient must be as small as we like, provided the chord is short enough.

Definition 2.51 Unit normal of a surface at a point (enotska normala ploskve v točki)

Let \(S\) be a set of points in space and \(P\) a point of \(S\). A unit vector \(\vek n\) is a unit normal (enotska normala) of the set \(S\) at the point \(P\) if for every number \(\eta > 0\) there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[|\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}| \le \eta\,|PQ| \tag{2.57}\]

for every point \(Q\) of \(S\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\). This is the same condition as (2.17) in definition 2.22, there with the sign \(<\), which is equivalent for arbitrary \(\eta\), here for an arbitrary set \(S\).

Source: The definition with chords is not from the sources. KREYSZIG §9.7 (PDF pp. 424-425) describes the normal of a surface at a point \(P\) as the perpendicular to the tangent plane, which is formed by the tangent vectors of the curves on the surface through \(P\).

The number \(\eta\) is the allowed cosine of the angle between the normal and a chord, and the number \(\delta\) tells how short the chords must be. The definition agrees with the old one. On a flat face, its unit normal has \(\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} = 0\) for every point \(Q\) of the face, so the inequality holds for every \(\delta\). Conversely, let \(\vek n\) be a normal of a flat face in the new sense and \(Q\) a point of the face to which a segment within the face leads from \(P\). All the points of this segment lie on the face, and the quotient \(\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}/|PQ|\) is the same for all of them, because the numerator and the denominator shrink by the same factor. Since for short enough chords its absolute value must be smaller than every \(\eta\), it is zero. The definition itself does not say whether a normal exists and how many there are. For level surfaces the next theorem answers.

Theorem 2.52 The gradient is perpendicular to the level surface (gradient je pravokoten na nivojsko ploskev)

Let the function of three variables \(f\) satisfy at the point \(P\) the assumptions of theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step: there is \(r > 0\) such that \(f\) is defined and has all three partial derivatives at all points that are less than \(r\) away from \(P\), and these derivatives are continuous at \(P\). Let \(S\) be the level surface of the function \(f\) at the value \(c = f(P)\) (definition 2.49) and let \(\nabla f(P) \neq \vek 0\). Then

\[\vek n = \frac{\nabla f(P)}{|\nabla f(P)|} \tag{2.58}\]

and \(-\vek n\) are unit normals of the set \(S\) at the point \(P\) (definition 2.51).

Proof

We must show that \(\vek n\) is a unit vector and that for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) for which (2.57) holds. We follow the steps on the shaft of figure 2.112.

  1. Since \(\nabla f(P) \neq \vek 0\), item 4 of lemma 2.12 gives \(|\nabla f(P)| > 0\), so we may divide by it. By items 3 and 4 of the same lemma, \(\vek n\cdot\vek n = \nabla f(P)\cdot\nabla f(P)/|\nabla f(P)|^2 = 1\), so \(\vek n\) is a unit vector (definition 1.18). On the shaft we divide the gradient \((6, 8, 0)\) by 10 and get \(\vek n = (0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\).
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\). We use theorem 1.89 with the error \(\eta\,|\nabla f(P)|\), which is positive. It gives us a \(\delta\) with \(0 < \delta \le r\) for which the remainder in (1.35) satisfies \(|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|\nabla f(P)|\,|PQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\), that is, for all sufficiently short steps from \(P\), also those that do not stay on the surface.
  3. Let \(Q\) be a point of \(S\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\), like the end of a chord in the figure. The points \(P\) and \(Q\) lie on the same level surface, so \(f(Q) = c = f(P)\) and the left side of (1.35) is zero.
  4. By (2.6) and (2.56) the three terms with derivatives on the right side of (1.35) are the scalar product of the gradient with the chord, \(\nabla f(P)\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}\). So the equation reads \(0 = \nabla f(P)\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} + R(Q)\), that is, \(\nabla f(P)\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} = -R(Q)\).
  5. We divide the equation by \(|\nabla f(P)|\). By item 3 of lemma 2.12, \(\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} = -R(Q)/|\nabla f(P)|\), and by step 2, \(|\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}| \le \eta\,|PQ|\). This is (2.57) for the vector \(\vek n\).
  6. For \(-\vek n\) we have \((-\vek n)\cdot(-\vek n) = \vek n\cdot\vek n = 1\) and \(|(-\vek n)\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}| = |\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) (the same lemma, item 3), so the same \(\delta\) serves for it too.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.7, theorem 2 (PDF p. 425). The source proves the theorem with the chain rule along curves that lie on the surface. The proof with the theorem on the change of a field is not from the source.

The proof showed that the zero change of the function along the surface forces short chords to be nearly perpendicular to the gradient, and that the deviation is just the remainder of the theorem on the change of a field. On the shaft we can write \(\delta\) down. The remainder is \(R(Q) = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 \le |PQ|^2\), so \(|\vek n\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}| = R(Q)/10 \le |PQ|^2/10\), and the inequality (2.57) holds with \(\delta = 10\,\eta\). For the chord to \(Q_1\) it is indeed \((9 + 1)/10 = 1{,}00\), and for the chord to \(Q_2\) it is \((2{,}56 + 0{,}64)/10 = 0{,}32\). At \(\eta = 0{,}01\) we get \(\delta = 0{,}1\) cm: all chords shorter than 1 mm differ from a right angle with \(\vek n\) by less than \(0{,}6^\circ\).

Which of the two normals is the outward one? The gradient points to where \(f\) grows: on a short step of length \(s\) in the direction of the gradient the scalar product with the gradient is \(s\,|\nabla f(P)| > 0\), and the remainder is small compared with it. For the shaft \(f\) is positive outside, so \(\vek n = \nabla f/|\nabla f|\) points out of the shaft and is its outward normal. For a wheel that grips the shaft from outside, the outward normal is \(-\vek n\). If we wrote the same surface with the equation \(25 - x^2 - y^2 = 0\), the gradient would point into the shaft. So we always check the direction with the value of the function at one point on each side of the surface. At any point of the surface of the shaft \(\nabla f = (2x, 2y, 0)\) with the length \(2\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 10\), so \(\vek n = (x/5,\ y/5,\ 0)\): the normal of a cylinder points straight away from the axis everywhere, as at the point \(P\).

Does the shaft have any other unit normal at the point \(P\)? It does not, and we show this directly. Let \(\vek m\) be a unit normal of the surface of the shaft at \(P\). Besides \(\vek n\) take the unit vectors \(\vek d = (-0{,}8;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\), the direction of the step from \(P\) to the point \(D\), and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). All three are perpendicular to each other.

  1. The point \(Q = (3, 4, 2 + h)\) lies on the surface for every \(h\), because \(f\) does not depend on \(z\). In the figure it is straight in front of the point \(P\) or behind it, along the line of sight. For it \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(|\vek m\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}|/|PQ| = |m_{\mathrm{z}}|\) for every \(h \neq 0\). By (2.57) this number must be smaller than every \(\eta > 0\), so \(m_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  2. For a point \(Q\) on the arc with \(z = 2\) we take \(\vek n\), \(\vek d\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) as the unit vectors of new axes. By lemma 2.45 on the components of a vector in turned axes, \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = q\,\vek n + p\,\vek d\) with \(q = \overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vek n\) and \(p = \overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vek d\), since the chord has no component along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The length is the same in both systems, so \(p^2 + q^2 = |PQ|^2\). Above we computed \(|q| \le |PQ|^2/10\). For chords shorter than 1 cm, therefore, \(|q| \le 0{,}1\,|PQ|\) and \(|p| \ge \sqrt{1 - 0{,}01}\,|PQ| > 0{,}99\,|PQ|\).
  3. For the same chord, from \(\vek m\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} = p\,(\vek m\cdot\vek d) + q\,(\vek m\cdot\vek n)\) and \(|\vek m\cdot\vek n| \le 1\) (corollary 2.15) it follows that \(0{,}99\,|PQ|\,|\vek m\cdot\vek d| \le |\vek m\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}| + |q| \le \eta\,|PQ| + |PQ|^2/10\) for short enough chords. We divide by \(|PQ|\): \(0{,}99\,|\vek m\cdot\vek d| \le \eta + |PQ|/10\). For a small \(\eta\) and a short chord the right side is as small as we like, so \(\vek m\cdot\vek d = 0\).
  4. So the vector \(\vek m\) is perpendicular to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and to \(\vek d\). In the axes with the unit vectors \(\vek n\), \(\vek d\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) it has, by the same lemma, only a component along \(\vek n\), and since it is a unit vector, \(\vek m = \vek n\) or \(\vek m = -\vek n\), that is, the blue arrow or its opposite.

So the chords along the axis and the chords around the circumference together fix the normal up to its sign. In general the same holds at every point of a level surface with a nonzero gradient, which follows from the implicit function theorem, which we do not prove here.

The assumption \(\nabla f(P) \neq \vek 0\) entered the proof in step 1, where we divide by the length of the gradient. It is not a mere formality. Take the function \(g(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 - z^2\). Its level surface \(g = 0\) is a cone with the apex \(O\) at the origin (figure 2.112, bottom right, the part above the apex is drawn). The gradient \(\nabla g = (2x, 2y, -2z)\) is \((0, 0, 0)\) at the apex, and the formula (2.58) would require division by zero. There is no normal there either. The directions \(\vek a = (1, 0, 1)\), \(\vek b = (-1, 0, 1)\) and \(\vek c = (0, 1, 1)\) lie on the cone: for the point \(Q = s\,\vek a\) we have \(g = s^2 + 0 - s^2 = 0\) for every \(s\), and the same for the other two. If \(\vek m\) were a unit normal at \(O\), the quotient \(\vek m\cdot\overrightarrow{OQ}/|OQ| = (m_{\mathrm{x}} + m_{\mathrm{z}})/\sqrt2\) would be the same for every \(s > 0\), so it would have to be zero. The three directions give \(m_{\mathrm{x}} + m_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(-m_{\mathrm{x}} + m_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(m_{\mathrm{y}} + m_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). From the first two \(m_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(m_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), from the third \(m_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so \(\vek m = \vek 0\), which is not a unit vector. At the tip the surface has no direction to face. The shaft has no such trouble: \(\nabla f = (2x, 2y, 0)\) is zero only on the axis, which is not on the surface.

In the lectures the function of the surface is written \(\varphi\), the surface with the equation \(\varphi = 0\) and the normal \(\vec n = \nabla\varphi/\lVert\nabla\varphi\rVert\). We write \(f\), because in this book \(\varphi\) is an angle.

Example: a wheel shrunk onto a shaft. Now we can use Cauchy's formula on a curved surface. The model is this. Onto a steel shaft of radius 5 cm, whose axis is the axis \(z\), a wheel is shrunk: we slip the heated wheel, whose hole is slightly too small, onto the shaft, and when it cools it grips the shaft. The wheel passes rotation on to the shaft and at the same time pushes it along the axis. Suppose that at the point \(P = (3, 4, 2)\) cm on the surface of the shaft the stress matrix (definition 2.48) is

\[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix} -80 & -40 & 10 \\ -40 & -20 & 30 \\ 10 & 30 & -50 \end{bmatrix} \text{MPa} .\]

The numbers are made up and chosen so that all six different components are nonzero and the calculation comes out even. The matrix is symmetric, as theorem 2.41 requires. The question: with what force per unit area does the wheel act on the shaft at \(P\), how much of it is perpendicular to the surface and how much along it?

First an assumption. In definition 2.20 we wrote the traction vector for a flat cut, but the surface of the shaft is curved. By Cauchy's postulate (definition 2.23) the traction vector on a curved surface at the point \(P\) equals the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) on the flat cut through \(P\) with the same unit normal \(\vek n\). Why is this justified here? On a patch of the surface with the side \(h\) around \(P\) a cylinder of radius \(R\) moves away from this plane by at most about \(h^2/(8R)\). For \(h = 1\) mm and \(R = 50\) mm this is \(0{,}0025\) mm, a four-hundredth of the side, and when we halve \(h\), this share halves. So in the limit of the definition the two patches no longer differ. That the traction vector depends only on the point and on the normal of the surface at it is also assumed by SADD (§3.2, PDF p. 65) and by BOWER, who describes the force per unit area of the surface of a body with the normal of the surface (BOWER §2.2.1, PDF p. 66). The assumption fails where the surface has no normal, for example at the edge where the surface of the shaft meets its end face. There the traction vector is not defined.

The calculation follows the chain surface, gradient, unit normal, product, parts.

  1. Surface. The surface of the shaft is the level surface \(f = 0\) of the function \(f = x^2 + y^2 - 25\), and \(P\) lies on it, \(9 + 16 - 25 = 0\).
  2. Gradient. \(\nabla f(P) = (6, 8, 0)\), the blue arrow in figure 2.112.
  3. Unit normal. By theorem 2.52, \(\vek n = (6, 8, 0)/10 = (0{,}6;\ 0{,}8;\ 0)\). It points out of the shaft, towards the wheel, in the direction \(\vek n\) in the figure.
  4. Product. By (2.54) we get the traction vector, whose first two components the blackwhite arrow shows:
    \[\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \begin{bmatrix} -80 \cdot 0{,}6 - 40 \cdot 0{,}8 + 10 \cdot 0 \\ -40 \cdot 0{,}6 - 20 \cdot 0{,}8 + 30 \cdot 0 \\ 10 \cdot 0{,}6 + 30 \cdot 0{,}8 - 50 \cdot 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -48 - 32 \\ -24 - 16 \\ 6 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -80 \\ -40 \\ 30 \end{bmatrix} \text{MPa} .\]
    The third column of the matrix is multiplied by \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). By (2.27) these are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), the stress vector on the face perpendicular to the axis \(z\). This vector does not enter the calculation, because the normal has no component \(z\). The numbers \(10\) and \(30\) do enter in the third row, as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\). On a face whose normal has no component \(z\) the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -50\) MPa does not act.
  5. Normal part. By (2.55), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek t\cdot\vek n = -80 \cdot 0{,}6 - 40 \cdot 0{,}8 = -48 - 32 = -80\) MPa. The sign is negative: the wheel presses on the shaft with 80 MPa. The normal part is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = (-48, -64, 0)\) MPa.
  6. Shear part. \(\vek t - \sigma_{\mathrm{n}}\vek n = (-80 + 48,\ -40 + 64,\ 30) = (-32, 24, 30)\) MPa. It is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), since \(-32 \cdot 0{,}6 + 24 \cdot 0{,}8 = -19{,}2 + 19{,}2 = 0\). Its size is the shear stress \(\tau = \sqrt{32^2 + 24^2 + 30^2} = \sqrt{1024 + 576 + 900} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\) MPa. (2.55) gives the same: \(|\vek t|^2 = 6400 + 1600 + 900 = 8900\) and \(\tau^2 = 8900 - 6400 = 2500\).
  7. Directions along the surface. On the surface of the shaft there are two natural directions at \(P\), perpendicular to \(\vek n\) and to each other: the direction around the circumference \(\vek d = (-0{,}8;\ 0{,}6;\ 0)\) and the direction of the axis \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The components of the shear part along them are \((-32) \cdot (-0{,}8) + 24 \cdot 0{,}6 = 25{,}6 + 14{,}4 = 40\) MPa and \(30\) MPa. So the shear part is \(40\,\vek d + 30\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Let us look at the result in figure 2.113. On the left we look along the axis of the shaft. The component \(t_{\mathrm{z}} = 30\) MPa points towards us and we do not see it, but we see the part \((t_{\mathrm{x}}, t_{\mathrm{y}}) = (-80, -40)\) MPa. It is drawn so that it ends at \(P\), because the wheel presses on the shaft. It is made of the normal part, which points straight towards the axis of the shaft \(O\), and the part \(40\,\vek d\) around the circumference. On the right we look at the patch of the surface around the point \(P\) from outside. We do not see the normal part here, because it points away from us, into the shaft. But we see the whole shear part: 40 MPa around the circumference and 30 MPa along the axis, which by the right triangle with sides 30, 40 and 50 give 50 MPa. The part around the circumference turns the shaft, the part along the axis pushes it. The whole traction vector has the size \(|\vek t| = \sqrt{80^2 + 50^2} = \sqrt{8900} = 94{,}3\) MPa.

Why the division by the length of the gradient in step 3? If we put the gradient itself into Cauchy's formula, we would get \(\ten\sigma\,\nabla f = (-800, -400, 300)\), ten times too much and in the unit MPa cm instead of MPa. Besides, the result would depend on how we wrote the surface: the equation \(2x^2 + 2y^2 - 50 = 0\) describes the same surface, but its gradient is twice as long. The unit normal is the same for both, and Cauchy's formula was derived in theorem 2.26 precisely for a unit normal.

2.9.4 Stress in turned axes

Now we can answer the first question from the beginning of the section. The component \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) in the new axes is the component \(l\) of the traction vector on the face perpendicular to the new axis \(k\). We know this vector from Cauchy's formula in the old axes, and its component along the new axis \(l\) we get by lemma 2.45 as the projection onto \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\). The indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(l\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The first two count the old axes, the other two the new ones.

Figure 2.114 shows the plane \(xy\) from above. The old axes are grey, the new axes, turned by the angle \(\theta\), are blue. Around the point \(P\) is a short face perpendicular to the new axis \(\bar x\), so \(k = x\). The traction vector \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}})\) acts on it. Cauchy's formula splits it into \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) and \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\), weighted by \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The projections of both parts onto the new axis \(\bar y\) add up to the projection of the whole vector, the component \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

Figure 2.115 shows what the double sum computes. The whole stress matrix \(\ten\sigma\) is in the middle. The row \(i\) holds the components of the vector \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\). The column \(l\) of \(\mat Q^\T\) is the row \(l\) of \(\mat Q\), so the new axis \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\). Their scalar product is the entry \((i, l)\) of the product \(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\). The row \(k\) of \(\mat Q\), the new axis \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), then adds these entries with the weights \(Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\) into the entry \((k, l)\) of the final matrix.

Theorem 2.53 Transformation of stress components (transformacija komponent napetosti)

Let \(P\) be a point of a body at which Cauchy's formula holds (theorem 2.26), \(\ten\sigma\) the stress matrix at \(P\) in the old rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) the stress matrix at \(P\) in the new system with the same unit of length, and \(\mat Q\) the rotation matrix from the old system to the new one. Then

\[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} , \qquad \bar{\ten\sigma} = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T . \tag{2.59}\]
Proof

We must show that the component \(l\) of the traction vector on the face with the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), written in the new system, equals the double sum.

  1. By definition 2.27 of the stress components, applied in the new system, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}}\) is the component \(l\) of the vector \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\) in the new system. By item 1 of lemma 2.45 on the components of a vector in turned axes this is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  2. The vector \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}})\) is determined by the force on a patch and its area, not by the choice of axes (definition 2.20), so we may compute it in the old system. Cauchy's formula holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, so also in the old one. We apply it to the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), which has the components \(Q_{\mathrm{kx}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{ky}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{kz}}\) in the old system (definition 2.44). By (2.25), \(\vek t(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  3. We substitute into step 1 and by items 2 and 3 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12) take out the numbers: \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\big(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\big)\).
  4. We compute the scalar product in the brackets with the components in the old system. By (2.26), \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{ix}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{iy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{iz}})\), by the definition of the rotation matrix \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = (Q_{\mathrm{lx}}, Q_{\mathrm{ly}}, Q_{\mathrm{lz}})\), and by (2.6) \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  5. We substitute step 4 into step 3 and get \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\).
  6. By definitions 1.101 and 1.99 the inner sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{jl}}\) is the entry in row \(i\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\). The outer sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)_{\mathrm{il}}\) is the entry in row \(k\) and column \(l\) of the product \(\mat Q\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)\). We do not write the brackets, because the matrix product is associative (item 2 of lemma 1.100 on the properties of the matrix product).

Source: CM (4.3.3) (PDF p. 186), SADD (3.3.1) (PDF p. 68). CM has the transposed stress matrix, but since \((\mat Q\,\ten\sigma^\T\mat Q^\T)^\T = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\), the rule has the same form in both conventions. The proof from Cauchy's formula is not from the sources.

The theorem says that for the components in the new axes we need no new reasoning about forces. The nine old components and the rotation matrix are enough, and every new component is a sum of nine products. The theorem needs no approximation and no property of the material, so it holds wherever Cauchy's formula holds. It also matters what the proof did not use: the symmetry of the stress components. So the rule also holds for a matrix that is not symmetric. When \(\ten\sigma\) is symmetric, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) is symmetric too. By lemma 1.102 on the transposed product, \(\bar{\ten\sigma}^\T = (\mat Q^\T)^\T\,\ten\sigma^\T\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T = \bar{\ten\sigma}\). This is as it must be, since the second condition of equilibrium, and with it the theorem on the symmetry of stress, holds in every right-handed coordinate system. For a mirrored system, for which we did not prove the theorem, this very computation gives the symmetry. The way back we get by multiplying both sides of (2.59) by \(\mat Q^\T\) from the left and by \(\mat Q\) from the right. Since \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) by (2.52), what remains is \(\ten\sigma = \mat Q^\T\bar{\ten\sigma}\,\mat Q\).

Figure 2.116 shows the turn about the axis \(z\) from above. The new axis \(\bar x\) has in the old axes the component \(c = \cos\theta\) along \(x\) and \(s = \sin\theta\) along \(y\), hence the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\). The new axis \(\bar y\) points perpendicular to it, its components are \(-s\) and \(c\). Between the axes \(x\) and \(\bar x\) is the angle \(\theta\). On the right is the square with the shear components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), which are equal by the symmetry theorem.

Most often we turn the axes about one of them. For the turn about the axis \(z\), the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(c\), \(s\), \(0\), and the row \(y\) the entries \(-s\), \(c\), \(0\). Let us compute \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by (2.59).

  1. For \(k = l = x\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{xi}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}}\). Since \(Q_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), only the terms in which \(i\) and \(j\) are \(x\) or \(y\) differ from zero:
    \[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xy}} + Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
  2. We substitute \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = s\): \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + sc\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} + s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\).
  3. By the theorem on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so the two middle terms combine into \(2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

In the same way we get the other components. We checked all of them with SymPy:

\[\begin{aligned} \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - 2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= -cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} . \end{aligned} \tag{2.60}\]

With \(c = \cos\theta\) and \(s = \sin\theta\) the first three lines are the formulas SADD (3.3.4) (PDF p. 68), and all of them are also written in CM (4.3.7) (PDF p. 187), where \(2cs\) and \(c^2 - s^2\) are expressed with the double angle.

Let us test the rule on the bar of section 2.2. This is a steel bar with a diameter of 10 mm, pulled at both ends by a force of 10 kN, with the axis \(x\) along the bar, the axis \(y\) up and the axis \(z\) toward us. Far from the ends the only nonzero stress component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) \(= 10\,000\ \text{N}/78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 127{,}32\) MPa (unrounded, section 2.2). We turn the axes about the axis \(z\) by the angle \(\theta\) with \(c = \cos\theta = 0{,}6\) and \(s = \sin\theta = 0{,}8\), so with \(c^2 = 0{,}36\), \(s^2 = 0{,}64\) and \(cs = 0{,}48\). By (2.60),

\[\begin{aligned} \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 0{,}36\,\sigma = 45{,}84\ \text{MPa} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= 0{,}64\,\sigma = 81{,}49\ \text{MPa} , \\ \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= -0{,}48\,\sigma = -61{,}12\ \text{MPa} , \end{aligned}\]

and all other components are zero (figure 2.117). In the old axes the point \(P\) is surrounded by a small square, in the new axes by a turned square around the same point \(P\). The old axes are drawn grey on the right, the new ones blue. On the faces perpendicular to the axis \(\bar x\) the normal stress \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}36\,\sigma\) acts, on the faces perpendicular to the axis \(\bar y\) the normal stress \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}64\,\sigma\). On all four faces there is also a shear component of size \(0{,}48\,\sigma\). Does this agree with section 2.4? The face with the normal \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0)\) is the oblique cut with \(\cos\theta = 0{,}6\). By (2.13) the normal stress on it is \(\sigma\cos^2\theta = 0{,}36\,\sigma\), and by (2.14) the shear stress is \(\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta = 0{,}48\,\sigma\). There we also computed that the shear part equals \(-\sigma\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\vek d\), where \(\vek d = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\) is exactly \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\). So its component along the axis \(\bar y\) is \(-0{,}48\,\sigma\), which is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Besides the size of the shear stress the rule also gives its direction: the shear part points opposite to the axis \(\bar y\).

The numbers hold one more pattern: \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}36\,\sigma\) and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}64\,\sigma\) add up to \(0{,}36\,\sigma + 0{,}64\,\sigma = \sigma\), as much as \(\sigma\) on the left. The normal stresses on faces whose normals enclose a right angle (in the bar \(\theta\) and \(\theta + 90^\circ\)) add up to \(\sigma\). In the table of section 2.4 we saw the same sum at \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), because \(\cos^2(\theta + 90^\circ) = \sin^2\theta = \cos^2(90^\circ - \theta)\). The first two lines of (2.60) tell why. When we add them, the terms \(2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(-2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) cancel, and what remains is \((c^2 + s^2)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). So in a turn about the axis \(z\) the sum \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) does not change. That in every turn the sum of all three diagonal components does not change we will show in section 2.11.

The second example is the pure shear of section 2.9.2: the cube is loaded only by forces along its faces, of size \(\tau_0\) per unit area, and the only nonzero stress components are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\). In section 2.6.6 we found with Cauchy's formula, face by face, that there is no shear on the faces perpendicular to the diagonals of the cube. Now we place the axes along the diagonals and compute all nine components at once. We look at the cube from the front as in figure 2.55, with the corners \(A\) bottom left, \(B\) bottom right, \(C\) top right and \(D\) top left. Let the new axis \(\bar x\) point along the diagonal from \(A\) toward \(C\), the new axis \(\bar z\) along the diagonal from \(B\) toward \(D\), and let the axis \(\bar y\) stay the axis \(y\):

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(1, 0, 1) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0) , \qquad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(-1, 0, 1) .\]

All three are unit vectors, for example \(|\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}|^2 = \tfrac12\,(1 + 0 + 1) = 1\), and pairwise perpendicular, for example \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac12\,(-1 + 0 + 1) = 0\). This is a turn about the axis \(y\) by an eighth of a full turn. We compute the product of three matrices in two steps.

  1. By definition 1.99 the entry \((i, l)\) of the product \(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\), that is, the scalar product of the row \(i\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) with the row \(l\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\), the vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\). The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\ten\sigma\) has the entries \(0\), \(0\), \(\tau_0\), and its scalar products with \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) are \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\), \(0\), \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\). The row \(y\) is zero. The row \(z\) has the entries \(\tau_0\), \(0\), \(0\), and its scalar products are \(\tau_0/\sqrt2\), \(0\), \(-\tau_0/\sqrt2\). So
    \[\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T = \frac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} .\]
  2. The entry \((k, l)\) of the product \(\mat Q\,(\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)\) is the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the row \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) and the column \(l\) of the matrix above. The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\). With the column \(x\) of the matrix above, with the entries \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), it gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(1 + 1) = \tau_0\), and with the column \(z\), with the entries \(\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(-\tfrac{\tau_0}{\sqrt2}\), it gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(1 - 1) = 0\). The row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(0\), \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\) and gives with the column \(x\) the number \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(-1 + 1) = 0\) and with the column \(z\) the number \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tfrac{\tau_0}{2}\,(-1 - 1) = -\tau_0\). The row \(y\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\) has the entries \(0\), \(1\), \(0\) and picks out the row \(y\) of the matrix above, which is zero. So
    \[\bar{\ten\sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} \tau_0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\tau_0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

In the axes along the diagonals the same stress has no shear component at all. On the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\) the tension \(\tau_0\) acts, and on the faces perpendicular to the diagonal \(BD\) the compression \(\tau_0\) (figure 2.118). For \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 50\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -50\) MPa. The sum of the diagonal components is zero before the turn and after it.

2.9.5 Strain in turned axes

Do the strain components also change by the same rule? In section 1.17 we got the components of the small strain tensor from the partial derivatives of the displacement field, \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) ((1.59)), where \(\mat H\) is the displacement gradient at the point \(P\) with the entries \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) (definition 1.112). Here \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) means the coordinate \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\). In the new axes the displacement has the components \(\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}\), which by lemma 2.45 we get from the old ones, and the points have the new coordinates \(\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\). The partial derivatives of the new components with respect to the new coordinates make up the matrix \(\bar{\mat H}\), and from it we get \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \tfrac12\,(\bar{\mat H} + \bar{\mat H}^\T)\). So first we must find out how the displacement gradient changes.

The idea is this. The partial derivative with respect to the new coordinate \(\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) is the limit of a quotient in which the point moves by a short step along the new axis \(l\). In the old axes this step is oblique, and the change of the displacement over a short step in any direction is given by theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step. So we need its hypotheses.

Figure 2.119 shows this step. Around the point \(P\) is a disc of radius \(r\), in which the displacements are defined. The step \(t\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\) leads from \(P\) to \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\), in the old axes it has the components \(t\,Q_{\mathrm{lx}}\) and \(t\,Q_{\mathrm{ly}}\). The displacement changes by the difference \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P_{\mathrm{t}}) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\). On the right this difference is drawn as a function of the step \(t\). The line with the slope \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\) is the main part, the band of width \(\eta\,|t|\) around it holds the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{i}}(t)\), and the number \(\delta\) says how far the band holds.

Lemma 2.54 Displacement gradient in turned axes (gradient pomikov v zasukanih oseh)

Let the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the displacement field in the old system satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step at the point \(P\): they are defined at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than some number \(r > 0\), their partial derivatives exist at these points and are continuous at \(P\). Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at \(P\) in the old system, \(\mat Q\) the rotation matrix from the old system to the new one, \(\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}\) the components of the displacement and \(\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) the coordinates in the new system. Then the partial derivatives \(\bar H_{\mathrm{kl}} = \partial\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) at \(P\) exist and

\[\bar{\mat H} = \mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T . \tag{2.61}\]
Proof

We must show that the limit that defines \(\partial\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) at \(P\) exists and equals the entry \((k, l)\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T\).

  1. By definition 1.26 of the partial derivative, applied in the new system, \(\partial\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) at \(P\) is the limit of the quotient \(\big(\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}(P_{\mathrm{t}}) - \bar u_{\mathrm{k}}(P)\big)/t\) as \(t\) approaches zero. The point \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) has the new coordinate \(\bar x_{\mathrm{l}}\) larger by \(t\) than \(P\) and the other two new coordinates equal. So the vector from \(P\) to \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) has in the new system the component \(l\) equal to \(t\) and the other two zero ((1.8)), and by lemma 1.21 \(P_{\mathrm{t}} = P + t\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  2. By item 1 of lemma 2.45, applied to the displacement vector at the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(P\), at every point \(\bar u_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,u_{\mathrm{i}}\). So the numerator of the quotient is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P + t\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\big)\).
  3. The step \(t\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\) has in the old system the components \(t\,Q_{\mathrm{lx}}\), \(t\,Q_{\mathrm{ly}}\), \(t\,Q_{\mathrm{lz}}\) (definition 2.44) and the length \(|t|\), because \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}\) is a unit vector. By theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, for every component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) and for \(0 < |t| < r\),
    \[u_{\mathrm{i}}(P + t\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{l}}) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,t\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} + R_{\mathrm{i}}(t) ,\]
    and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}(t)| \le \eta\,|t|\) for every \(t\) with \(0 < |t| < \delta\). For all three components at once we take the smallest of the three bands \(\delta\).
  4. We substitute step 3 into step 2 and divide by \(t\). The quotient is
    \[\frac{\bar u_{\mathrm{k}}(P_{\mathrm{t}}) - \bar u_{\mathrm{k}}(P)}{t} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\frac{R_{\mathrm{i}}(t)}{t} .\]
    The first double sum does not depend on \(t\). We call it \(d\).
  5. We write the definition of the limit 1.5 for this quotient and the number \(d\). We choose an error \(\eta' > 0\) and take \(\eta = \eta'/4\) in step 3. Every entry \(Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is a component of the unit vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{k}}\), so \(|Q_{\mathrm{ki}}| \le 1\), as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 2.26. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), for \(0 < |t| < \delta\)
    \[\Big|\sum_{\mathrm{i}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\frac{R_{\mathrm{i}}(t)}{t}\Big| \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |Q_{\mathrm{ki}}|\,\frac{|R_{\mathrm{i}}(t)|}{|t|} \le 3\,\eta = \tfrac34\,\eta' < \eta' .\]
    So the difference between the quotient and the number \(d\) is less than \(\eta'\), as the definition of the limit requires.
  6. So the limit exists and equals \(d = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\). As in step 6 of the proof of theorem 2.53 on the transformation of stress components, this is the entry \((k, l)\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T\).

Source: CM (2.5.21) (PDF p. 87) gives the same rule for components in general, BOWER Appendix B.1.1 (PDF p. 756) takes the gradient as the first example of a quantity with such a rule. The proof with the theorem on the change of a field is not from the sources.

From the gradient we get the strains at once.

Figure 2.120 splits the gradient into two parts. Under the gradient \(\mat H\) a small square becomes a parallelogram. The symmetric part \(\ten\varepsilon\) stretches the square in one direction and shrinks it in the other, the antisymmetric part \(\ten\omega\) only turns it.

Lemma 2.55 Transformation of strain components (transformacija komponent deformacije)

Under the hypotheses of lemma 2.54 the matrix of the small strain tensor at the point \(P\) in the new system is

\[\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T . \tag{2.62}\]
Proof

We must show that the rule for the gradient gives the same rule for its symmetric part.

  1. By (1.59), written in the new system, \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \tfrac12\,(\bar{\mat H} + \bar{\mat H}^\T)\).
  2. By lemma 2.54,
    \[\bar{\mat H} = \mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T .\]
    Transposing, by lemma 1.102 on the transposed product, used twice, and \((\mat Q^\T)^\T = \mat Q\), gives
