    \[\bar{\mat H}^\T = \mat Q\,\mat H^\T\mat Q^\T .\]
  3. We substitute into step 1: \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \tfrac12\,(\mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T + \mat Q\,\mat H^\T\mat Q^\T)\).
  4. By distributivity and taking out the number (item 3 of lemma 1.100 on the matrix product) we take \(\mat Q\) out on the left and \(\mat Q^\T\) on the right:
    \[\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\tfrac12\,(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\,\mat Q^\T .\]
    The expression in the brackets is \(\ten\varepsilon\), so
    \[\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T .\]

Source: SADD (2.3.1) (PDF p. 47), CM (3.4.29) (PDF p. 135).

The rule is exact for the matrix defined by (1.59). This matrix, however, describes the deformation well only when the partial derivatives of the displacements are small (section 1.17). The same four steps with a minus instead of a plus give \(\bar{\ten\omega} = \mat Q\,\ten\omega\,\mat Q^\T\) for the small rotation tensor \(\ten\omega = \tfrac12\,(\mat H - \mat H^\T)\) (definition 1.122). The Green-Lagrange strain tensor \(\mat E = \tfrac12\,(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I)\) ((1.54)) also changes by the same rule, without the assumption of small derivatives. Since \(\mat I = \mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\), the deformation gradient in the new system is \(\bar{\mat F} = \mat I + \bar{\mat H} = \mat Q\,(\mat I + \mat H)\,\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\mat F\,\mat Q^\T\), so \(\bar{\mat F}^\T\bar{\mat F} = \mat Q\,\mat F^\T\mat Q^\T\mat Q\,\mat F\,\mat Q^\T = \mat Q\,\mat F^\T\mat F\,\mat Q^\T\) and \(\bar{\mat E} = \mat Q\,\mat E\,\mat Q^\T\) (CM (3.4.29), PDF p. 135).

Let us test the lemma on the sheared cube of section 1.6.2. A steel cube with the edge \(h = 10\) mm is glued to a table by its bottom face, and its top face was pushed by \(s = 10\) µm in the direction of the axis \(x\). The origin is at the bottom front left corner \(A\), the axis \(z\) points up, and the displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The only nonzero partial derivative is \(H_{\mathrm{xz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = 0{,}001\), so by (1.59) the only nonzero strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = 0{,}0005\). The matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\) has the same form as the stress matrix of pure shear, only with the number \(0{,}0005\) instead of \(\tau_0\). So in the axes along the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) of the front face, by the same computation,

\[\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -0{,}0005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The number \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}0005\) is the strain of the fibre along the diagonal \(AC\), and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}0005\) the strain of the fibre along the diagonal \(BD\). In the table of section 1.6.2 we computed exactly, from the lengths of the fibres, \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The difference comes from the squares of the derivatives, which the small strain tensor leaves out. In the diagonal axes there are no shear components. The same deformation that is shear in the axes \(x\) and \(z\) is stretching in one direction and shortening in the other in the axes along the diagonals (figure 2.121), as section 1.1 announced. The figure shows the front face of the cube with its vertices before loading and in orange after it. The axes are \(x\) and \(z\). A small square along the axes becomes a parallelogram, a small square along the diagonals becomes an almost rectangle.

We can also check the lemma directly, without matrices. A point has the new coordinates \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\), and its old coordinates are the components of the vector from the origin \(A\) to the point, so by item 2 of lemma 2.45 \(z = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(\bar x + \bar z)\). By item 1 of the same lemma the new components of the displacement are

\[\begin{aligned} \bar u_{\mathrm{x}} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(u_{\mathrm{x}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}) = 0{,}0005\,(\bar x + \bar z) , \\ \bar u_{\mathrm{y}} &= 0 , \\ \bar u_{\mathrm{z}} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,(-u_{\mathrm{x}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}) = -0{,}0005\,(\bar x + \bar z) . \end{aligned}\]

The partial derivatives with respect to the new coordinates are \(\partial\bar u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial\bar x = \partial\bar u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial\bar z = 0{,}0005\) and \(\partial\bar u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial\bar x = \partial\bar u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial\bar z = -0{,}0005\), and all others are zero. These are the entries of the matrix \(\mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T\), as the lemma requires (we checked with SymPy). The symmetric part of this matrix is \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon}\) above. The antisymmetric part has only the entries \(\bar\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\) and \(\bar\omega_{\mathrm{zx}} = -0{,}0005\) and describes a turn without a change of shape (definition 1.122): besides stretching and shortening, the diagonals also turn a little.

What about the strain of a single fibre? By (1.61) the strain of a short fibre in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) is approximately \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\). In the new system the same direction has the components \(\bar{\vek n} = \mat Q\,\vek n\), and by lemma 1.102 and by (2.52)

\[\bar{\vek n}^\T\bar{\ten\varepsilon}\,\bar{\vek n} = \vek n^\T\mat Q^\T\,\mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T\,\mat Q\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n .\]

In both systems we get the same number, as must be, since the strain of a fibre is the ratio of two lengths, and lengths do not depend on the axes. The same holds for the normal stress on a given face, \(\bar{\vek n}^\T\bar{\ten\sigma}\,\bar{\vek n} = \vek n^\T\ten\sigma\,\vek n\), which section 2.3 announced with the words that the stresses computed with the scalar product do not depend on how we place the axes. The converse holds too. The strains of the fibres in all directions determine all six components. The component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is given by the fibre along the axis \(x\), and the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), by section 1.17.4, by the fibre along the diagonal between the axes \(x\) and \(y\) together with the fibres along the two axes: the diagonal stretches by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) more than the average of those two fibres. Since the strains of the fibres are the same in both systems, the components in the new system are determined, and the rule (2.62) is the only one that makes this possible.

2.9.6 The change of a right angle

Definition 1.3 says that the shear strain of two perpendicular directions describes how the right angle between them changes. In section 1.17 we got the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x)\) from partial derivatives, and in section 1.17.4 we found its geometric meaning only to first order, with the tangents of the tilts of the fibres. Here we derive it from the scalar product with an error estimate, where we compute angles from components. The angle between two vectors comes from the scalar product: for the angle \(\varphi\) between nonzero vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\), \(\cos\varphi = \vek a\cdot\vek b/(|\vek a|\,|\vek b|)\) (section 2.3, KREYSZIG §9.2 (4), PDF p. 388).

The model is this. The point \(P\) lies in a body whose displacement field satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step. From the point \(P\) we draw two short fibres of the same length \(h\), in the directions of the unit vectors \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\), which are perpendicular, \(\vek m\cdot\vek n = 0\). The vectors of the fibres before loading are \(h\,\vek m\) and \(h\,\vek n\). After loading, by section 1.17, the vectors of the fibres are \(h\,\mat F\vek m\) and \(h\,\mat F\vek n\), where \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) is the deformation gradient ((1.47)), each up to a remainder that is small compared with \(h\). The point \(P\) moves to \(P_1\), and the old directions are drawn from \(P_1\) grey dashed. We define \(\varphi\) as the limit of the angle between the fibres as \(h\) tends to zero. By theorem 1.89 the remainders are at most \(\eta h\) for an arbitrarily small \(\eta\), so after dividing by \(h\) the fibre vectors tend to \(\mat F\vek m\) and \(\mat F\vek n\), and \(\cos\varphi\) is the quotient written below. How large is the angle \(\varphi\) between the fibres after loading (figure 2.123)?

  1. By the formula for the cosine, for the angle \(\varphi\) between the fibre vectors after loading, \(\cos\varphi = (h\,\mat F\vek m)\cdot(h\,\mat F\vek n)/\big(|h\,\mat F\vek m|\,|h\,\mat F\vek n|\big)\). By item 3 of the properties of the scalar product the numerator is \(h^2\,(\mat F\vek m)\cdot(\mat F\vek n)\). By (1.10) the length of the multiple is \(|h\,\mat F\vek m| = \sqrt{h^2\,|\mat F\vek m|^2} = h\,|\mat F\vek m|\), because \(h > 0\), and likewise for \(\vek n\). The factor \(h^2\) cancels:
    \[\cos\varphi = \frac{(\mat F\vek m)\cdot(\mat F\vek n)}{|\mat F\vek m|\,|\mat F\vek n|} .\]
  2. From \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) and \(\mat I\vek m = \vek m\) (definition 1.108), the fibre vector after loading is \(\mat F\vek m = \vek m + \mat H\vek m\), that is, \(\mat H\vek m\) is added to the fibre before loading, and likewise \(\mat F\vek n = \vek n + \mat H\vek n\).
  3. By item 2 of the properties of the scalar product we expand: \((\vek m + \mat H\vek m)\cdot(\vek n + \mat H\vek n) = \vek m\cdot\vek n + \vek m\cdot(\mat H\vek n) + (\mat H\vek m)\cdot\vek n + (\mat H\vek m)\cdot(\mat H\vek n)\).
  4. The first term is zero, because the directions are perpendicular.
  5. The second term is \(\vek m\cdot(\mat H\vek n) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} m_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the third is
    \[(\mat H\vek m)\cdot\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,m_{\mathrm{j}}\Big)\,n_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
    The names of the indices \(i\) and \(j\) only count, so in the third we swap them:
    \[(\mat H\vek m)\cdot\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} m_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
    By (1.59) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\), so the sum of the two terms is
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} m_{\mathrm{i}}\,(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = 2 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} m_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = 2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n .\]
  1. Up to here the computation is exact: \((\mat F\vek m)\cdot(\mat F\vek n) = 2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + (\mat H\vek m)\cdot(\mat H\vek n)\).
  2. Now we use that the derivatives are small, in size below \(0{,}001\). Steel has this order of size as long as it does not yield, since its strains are then below about \(0{,}0011\) (section 2.2). The components of the unit vectors \(\vek m\) and \(\vek n\) are in size at most \(1\). The term \(2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) is a sum of derivatives multiplied by components, and the last term \((\mat H\vek m)\cdot(\mat H\vek n)\) a sum of products of two derivatives multiplied by components. The denominator is almost \(1\). The square of the length is \(|\mat F\vek m|^2 = 1 + 2\,\vek m\cdot(\mat H\vek m) + |\mat H\vek m|^2\), so \(|\mat F\vek m|\) differs from \(1\) by about \(\vek m\cdot(\mat H\vek m)\), a sum of derivatives multiplied by components, and likewise \(|\mat F\vek n|\). The numerator is itself a sum of terms with derivatives, so when we replace the denominator by \(1\), the fraction changes only by terms with products of two derivatives. If we leave out all terms with products of two derivatives, what remains is
    \[\cos\varphi \approx 2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n .\]
    We may do this only when \(2\,\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\) is not itself as small as these products. What this means in numbers, step 8 shows for a pair of axes.
  3. For \(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), only the term with \(m_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) in the double sum differs from zero, so \(\vek m^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\cos\varphi \approx 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). For this pair we estimate the error in numbers. By (1.39) the vector \(\mat H\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the components \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{zx}}\), and the vector \(\mat H\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the components \(H_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{zy}}\). The last term we left out is therefore \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}H_{\mathrm{xy}} + H_{\mathrm{yx}}H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zx}}H_{\mathrm{zy}}\), a sum of three products of two derivatives, and it is in size below \(3 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Since \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\mat H\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = H_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), by the square of the length in step 7 \(|\mat F\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}|\) differs from \(1\) by about \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and \(|\mat F\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}|\) by about \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and both strains are in size below \(0{,}001\). When we replace the denominator by \(1\), the fraction therefore changes by at most about two thousandths of its value. When \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is about \(0{,}001\), both errors are only a few millionths, a few hundred times less than \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). When \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) itself is only a few millionths, however, the term we left out can be larger than \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and the formula can even give the wrong sign.

The figure shows how large the error is. Above is the denominator, a band between \(0{,}998\) and \(1{,}002\) around \(1\), because each of the two lengths differs from \(1\) by less than \(0{,}001\). Below is the axis of values of \(\cos\varphi\), on it the approximation \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}001\) and beside it the two errors, each only a few millionths, so they are barely visible in the figure. For a small shear strain, however, the error and the value are equally large.

The angle \(\varphi\) is close to a right angle. We call the decrease of the right angle \(\gamma = 90^\circ - \varphi\). From school trigonometry, \(\cos(90^\circ - \gamma) = \sin\gamma\), as in section 2.4, so

\[\sin\gamma \approx 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} . \tag{2.63}\]

So twice the shear strain is approximately the sine of the angle by which the right angle between the fibres along the axes \(x\) and \(y\) decreases. The sign tells the direction: for a positive \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\cos\varphi > 0\) and the angle decreases, for a negative one it increases, provided \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is not as small as the omitted products (step 8). SADD describes the sign of the shear strain in the same way (PDF p. 43). The same derivation with \(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) gives \(\sin\gamma \approx 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), and with the other pairs of axes the other two shear components.

CM and SADD say the same even more briefly: \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is simply the decrease of the right angle, measured in radians (CM (3.5.8), (3.5.9), PDF p. 142, SADD (2.2.3), PDF p. 43). We defined the radian with the normal and shear strain (definition 1.3) as the length of an arc on a circle of radius \(1\). For a small angle \(\sin\gamma \approx \gamma\), as CM also takes (PDF p. 142). At \(\gamma = 0{,}001\) rad, \(\sin\gamma = 0{,}0009999998\), a difference of only \(1{,}7 \cdot 10^{-10}\) (computed with NumPy), more than ten thousand times smaller than the errors of step 8, which are a few millionths. So (2.63) gives back the result of chapter 1 that the right angle decreases by \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) radians, now with the error estimate of step 8. This is why books call the number \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the engineering shear strain (inženirska strižna deformacija) (CM, PDF p. 141, SADD, PDF p. 43), and our component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is half of it. Without the assumption of small derivatives, the computation up to step 6 is exact also with the Green-Lagrange strain tensor. Since \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I + 2\,\mat E\) ((1.54)), \((\mat F\vek m)\cdot(\mat F\vek n) = \vek m^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n = 2\,\vek m^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) and \(\cos\varphi = 2\,\vek m^\T\mat E\,\vek n/(|\mat F\vek m|\,|\mat F\vek n|)\) (CM (3.5.7), (3.5.8), PDF p. 142).

Let us test it on the sheared cube, at the corner \(A\) between the edges \(AB\) along the axis \(x\) and \(AD\) along the axis \(z\) (figure 2.123, right), with the axes \(x\) and \(z\). Here \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\). The edge \(AD\) tilts to \(AD_1\) and the right angle decreases by \(\gamma\). Exactly, from the vectors of the edges of section 1.6.2, \((10\,000, 0, 0)\) and \((10, 0, 10\,000)\) in micrometres, we get

\[\cos\varphi = \frac{10\,000 \cdot 10 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 10\,000}{10\,000 \cdot 10\,000{,}005} = 0{,}0009999995 .\]

The approximation \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\) from formula (2.63) differs from the exact value by only \(5 \cdot 10^{-10}\). For the cube the displacement field is linear, so there is no remainder in the derivation at all. The last term of step 6 is zero too, because the only nonzero derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = 0{,}001\), and so \(\mat H\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\). The difference comes only from the denominator, which we replaced by \(1\): \(|\mat F\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}| = \sqrt{1 + 0{,}001^2} = 1{,}0000005\), and \(0{,}001/1{,}0000005 = 0{,}0009999995\). The right angle decreased by \(\gamma = 0{,}0573^\circ\) (computed with NumPy). Between the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\), however, \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\) in the diagonal axes, and the formula predicts that the right angle between them stays. Exactly, the vectors of the diagonals after loading are \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\) and \((-9\,990, 0, 10\,000)\), their scalar product is \(10\,010 \cdot (-9\,990) + 10\,000 \cdot 10\,000 = -99\,999\,900 + 100\,000\,000 = 100\), since \(10\,010 \cdot 9\,990 = (10\,000 + 10)(10\,000 - 10) = 10\,000^2 - 10^2\), and the cosine of the angle between them is \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), two thousand times less than between the edges. The angle between the diagonals changes only by a term with the square of the shift.

Formula (2.63) holds as long as the partial derivatives of the displacements are small, also those that describe a turn, and as long as the shear strain is not as small as the squares of the derivatives. For large strains or large turns we use the exact formula with \(\mat E\) and with the lengths \(|\mat F\vek m|\) and \(|\mat F\vek n|\).

2.9.7 Tensors

Let us collect what we have derived. The figure shows one arrow \(\vek a\) in the old axes and in the new axes, turned by the angle \(\theta\). Its components in the old axes are \(3\) and \(2\), and in the new ones \(3{,}4\) and \(-1{,}2\). The components of a vector change in the passage to a new system by the rule \(\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q\,\vek a\). The matrices of the stress, of the small strain tensor, of the displacement gradient and of the small rotation tensor change by the rule \(\bar{\mat A} = \mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T\), like the stress of the bar, which has other components in the turned axes. Lengths, for example the length of the arrow, scalar products, the normal stress on a given face and the strain of a given fibre do not change. In section 1.5.5 we wrote that a vector in mechanics is a quantity whose components change in a definite way when the axes are turned, while the arrow stays the same, and then we could not say in what way. Now we know. The same can be said for quantities with nine components.

From history

In his lectures on quaternions, printed in Dublin in 1853, Hamilton wrote every quaternion \(q\) as a product of two factors, \(q = Tq \times Uq\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 163). He called the first, \(Tq\), the tensor (tenzor), and it was only a number that stretches a unit vector to the right length (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 163). The word then had no connection with a directed quantity. According to TIMO, the notions of tensor and tensor-triad (tenzorska trojica) were first introduced into the theory of elasticity by Woldemar Voigt, who as professor at Göttingen specially studied the elastic properties of crystals (TIMO, PDF p. 284 and 286). LOVE writes that any strain is equivalent to three simple extensions along three perpendicular directions without shear, which we shall meet in section 2.11. It was proposed to call a quantity that is equivalent to its components in the same way as a simple extension a tensor. A quantity that is equivalent to its components in the same way as a strain should be called a tensor-triad (LOVE, PDF p. 61). Today's meaning differs from Hamilton's, since a tensor is itself a directed quantity of a general type, which in special cases is an ordinary vector (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 163).

Let us return to the quantities with nine components.

Definition 2.56 Second-order tensor (tenzor drugega reda)

In mechanics a second-order tensor (tenzor drugega reda) is a quantity that in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system is described by nine numbers, its components \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), collected in the matrix \(\mat A\), and whose components change in the passage from the old system to another such system with the same unit of length by the rule

\[\bar{\mat A} = \mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T , \qquad \bar A_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}} , \tag{2.64}\]

where \(\mat Q\) is the rotation matrix from the old system to the new one. A quantity with three components that change by the rule \(\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q\,\vek a\) is a first-order tensor (tenzor prvega reda), and a quantity with a single component that does not change is a zero-order tensor (tenzor ničtega reda).

Source: SADD (1.5.1) (PDF p. 18), CM (2.5.21) (PDF p. 87).

So a first-order tensor is a vector in the sense of mechanics, and a zero-order tensor is a scalar, for example the length of a fibre or the normal stress on a given face. By theorem 2.53 the stress at a point is a second-order tensor, and this is why books call it the stress tensor (napetostni tenzor), which in section 2.6.5 we only mentioned. By lemmas 2.54 and 2.55 the displacement gradient and the small strain tensor are second-order tensors too, and by the same computation so are the small rotation tensor and the Green-Lagrange strain tensor. So stress and strain are quantities of the same kind, although the first measures forces and the second a change of shape.

Just as a vector is not the triple of its components, a tensor is not the matrix of its components. The stress at a point is one, but its matrix depends on how we place the axes: it is different in the old axes and in the turned ones. SADD says it in words: the components of the stress tensor change with the choice of coordinates, but the tensor itself, which describes the state of stress at the point, does not (SADD, PDF pp. 18-19). Since the rule (2.64) gives the components in every other system from the components in one, it is enough to know a tensor in a single system.

May we prescribe the components of a tensor in each system as we like? No. Suppose someone claimed that the stress at some point is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 127{,}32\) MPa in every coordinate system, with all other components zero. The bar of section 2.9.4 shows that this cannot be true. On its small square in the old axes only the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 127{,}32\) MPa acts. In the blue axes, turned with \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), the turned square of the same point carries \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 45{,}84\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 81{,}49\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -61{,}12\) MPa. By contrast, the matrix \(-p\,\mat I\) of the fluid at rest of section 2.6.6 has the same components in every system, since by (2.52) \(\mat Q\,(-p\,\mat I)\,\mat Q^\T = -p\,\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = -p\,\mat I\). This is the fact that the pressure in a fluid at rest is the same in all directions, written with the rule. CM states that every second-order tensor that has the same components in all systems is a multiple of the matrix \(\mat I\) (CM, PDF p. 87).

Our definition is a special form of a more general concept, and let us say in what way. First, it holds only for rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems, so books call such tensors Cartesian tensors (kartezični tenzorji) (SADD §1.5, PDF p. 18). The word tensor without an adjective generally means a concept in which the coordinates are not necessarily rectangular Cartesian, for example cylindrical, and the components change by other rules (SADD, PDF p. 19). Second, mathematics defines a second-order tensor without coordinates, as a linear map whose input is a vector and whose output is a vector (BOWER Appendix B.1.1, PDF p. 756). Linear means that it maps the sum of two vectors to the sum of their images: the vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) give the sum, their images \(T\vek a\) and \(T\vek b\) give the same sum, the image of the sum. A multiple of a vector to the same multiple of its image, as holds for the product with a matrix by lemma 1.98. The stress tensor maps the unit normal \(\vek n\) to the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\vek n\), and the displacement gradient maps a short step \(\vek h\) to the linear part of the difference of displacements \(\mat H\vek h\) (the difference is \(\mat H\vek h\) up to a remainder that is small compared with \(|\vek h|\)), both at the same point. The matrix is the record of such a map in a chosen system, and the rule (2.64) tells how the record of the same map changes when we change the system. Third, there are also tensors of higher orders, with components with more indices and with a rule in which one factor \(Q\) appears for each index (SADD (1.5.1), PDF p. 18). In chapter 3 we will meet a quantity with four indices that relates stress to strain.

From history

The development of electrodynamics and the theory of relativity gave great importance to the calculus of tensors, as used by the general notion of the previous paragraph (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 163). It was developed chiefly by G. Ricci and T. Levi-Civita in 1901, and later by Albert Einstein and others (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 164).

2.9.8 Mathematics: index notation

The equilibrium equations (2.38) are three lines with three derivatives each, and the rule (2.64) is a double sum. Books on elasticity and the lectures write such equations in one short line, in index notation (indeksni zapis). In this book we write the sums out, because a written-out sum shows every term, and it will stay so. This section is a dictionary that tells how to read a short line back into written-out sums. It says nothing new about mechanics, and no proof in the book needs it. Where an equation in the book has both forms, the toolbar button Index notation switches between them.

We build the dictionary on the equilibrium equations, which we already know (figure 2.127). At the top is the short line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), at the bottom are the three written-out equations of the theorem on the equilibrium equations. The short line uses three conventions. The first: the index \(\ix{i}\) stands exactly once in every term. Such an index is free, and the line holds for each of its values separately. The short line is therefore three equations, one for each of \(\ix{i} = x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The second: the index \(\ix{j}\) stands twice in the same term, once on the stress and once after the comma. Such an index means the sum over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and the sign \(\sum\) is not written. In the first equation these are three derivatives, for \(\ix{j} = x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The third: the comma before an index means the partial derivative with respect to the coordinate with that index.

The last convention needs a coordinate with an index. So books number the axes: \(x_1 = x\), \(x_2 = y\), \(x_3 = z\), the unit vectors of the axes are \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\), and the indices run over \(1\), \(2\), \(3\). The component \(\sigma_{11}\) is our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the component \(\sigma_{12}\) our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the component \(u_3\) our \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). In this book the indices run over the letters \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and when we need a coordinate with an index, we write \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\), as in lemma 1.134. The denominator \(\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the figure is thus, for \(\ix{j} = y\), simply \(\partial y\). The meaning is the same with numbers and with letters.

Definition 2.57 Index notation and the summation convention (indeksni zapis in sumacijski dogovor)

Let the quantities be written by components in a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and let the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) (with numbered axes over \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), where \(x_1 = x\), \(x_2 = y\), \(x_3 = z\)). Index notation (indeksni zapis) is the notation with these conventions:

  1. An index that stands exactly once in a term is a free index (prosti indeks). The equation holds for each value of the free index separately, and all terms of the equation have the same free indices.
  2. An index that stands exactly twice in a term is a dummy index (nemi indeks). It means the sum of the term over all three values of this index, and the sign \(\sum\) is not written (summation convention, sumacijski dogovor):
    \[a_{\mathrm{i}}\,b_{\mathrm{i}} \ \ \text{means}\ \ \sum_{\mathrm{i}} a_{\mathrm{i}}\,b_{\mathrm{i}} = a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{z}} .\]
  3. No index stands more than twice in a term.
  4. A comma before an index means the partial derivative with respect to the coordinate with that index (comma derivative, odvod z vejico), and two indices after the comma two successive derivatives:
    \[f_{,\mathrm{i}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{kl}} = \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} .\]

A term is a product that plus signs, minus signs or the equals sign separate from its neighbours.

Source: SADD §1.2, (1.2.6) (PDF pp. 12-13), the comma derivative in §1.8 (PDF p. 25). CM §2.2.5 (PDF pp. 52-53).

The name dummy index says that the letter itself means nothing: \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\,b_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\,b_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the same sum \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\), so we may rename a dummy index to any letter that the term does not yet have (CM, PDF p. 53). A free index we may not, because it tells which of the three equations we are reading. In the figure we could replace the orange \(\ix{j}\) by \(\ix{k}\), but the blue \(\ix{i}\) only in all terms at once.

Let us read four lines, two that are correct and two that are not.

  • \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\). The index \(\ix{i}\) is free, \(\ix{j}\) is a dummy, so these are three equations with three terms each, \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\) and two more. This is Cauchy's formula (2.27), and it reads the same way as the rows in the figure, only without derivatives.
  • \(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{i}}\). The index \(\ix{i}\) stands twice, so there is no free index and the line is a single number, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\). If \(\vek u\) is the displacement field, this is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), the approximate relative change of volume from section 1.17. A trap hides here: in index notation \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ii}}\) is not one diagonal component but the sum of all three.
  • \(a_{\mathrm{i}} = b_{\mathrm{j}}\) is not an allowed line. On the left the free index is \(\ix{i}\), on the right \(\ix{j}\), and the line does not say which component is compared with which (SADD, PDF p. 13). In the figure the blue index stands in both terms, and this is exactly what is missing here.
  • \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\,b_{\mathrm{i}}\,c_{\mathrm{i}}\) is not an allowed line, because \(\ix{i}\) stands three times and it is not determined what we sum (SADD, PDF p. 13). In the figure the dummy index stands exactly twice, and the convention allows no more. The sum \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{z}}\) must be written with the sign \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Outside this section the book does not use the summation convention. In the written-out notation of the book a repeated index does not mean a sum: in section 1.17.5, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = \tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{ii}} - H_{\mathrm{ii}}) = 0\) is a statement about each diagonal element separately. The sum by convention holds only in the second form of an equation, which the button Index notation shows, and in this section. To make the difference visible, here we write every equation first with the sign \(\sum\) and only then by the convention.

In the lectures the axes are numbered, the body force per unit volume is \(f_{\mathrm{i}}\) in place of \(b_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the equations of motion from section 2.7.9 are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + f_{\mathrm{i}} = \rho\,a_{\mathrm{i}}\).

The Kronecker delta. In index notation the identity matrix gets its own sign. Let us see why it is useful. In section 2.10 we shall write the equality \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \tau_0\,\vek n\) as \((\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I)\,\vek n = \vek 0\), and for this we need \(\vek n = \mat I\,\vek n\). By components this is \(n_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} I_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\). In index notation the elements of the identity matrix are written \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Definition 2.58 Kronecker delta (Kroneckerjeva delta)

The Kronecker delta (Kroneckerjeva delta) is the nine numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where the indices \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\):

\[\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1 \ \ \text{for}\ \ \ix{i} = \ix{j} , \qquad \delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0 \ \ \text{for}\ \ \ix{i} \neq \ix{j} .\]

These are the elements of the identity matrix of order \(3\) from definition 1.108, \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = I_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: SADD (1.3.1) (PDF p. 15), CM (2.2.47) (PDF p. 54).

Let us draw these nine numbers (figure 2.128). The table has rows for \(\ix{i} = x\), \(y\), \(z\) and columns for \(\ix{j} = x\), \(y\), \(z\). On the diagonal, where the indices are equal, there are ones, in the six other cells zeros. The table does not change if we exchange rows and columns, so \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ji}}\). What the delta does in a sum, the right side of the figure shows. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{yj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\) has three terms. In two of them the delta is zero, because its indices are different, and the terms drop out. The term that remains is the one with \(\ix{j} = y\), with the delta \(1\), and the sum is \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\). So the delta has picked, from three components, the one whose index equals its second index. The same holds for every free index.

Lemma 2.59 Substitution rule for the Kronecker delta (pravilo zamenjave za Kroneckerjevo delto)

Let the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) as in the table. For any three numbers \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\) and any matrix \(\mat A\) of size \(3 \times 3\):

  1. the delta replaces an index: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}} = a_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,A_{\mathrm{jk}} = A_{\mathrm{ik}}\), in index notation \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}} = a_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,A_{\mathrm{jk}} = A_{\mathrm{ik}}\),
  2. the sum of the diagonal elements is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \delta_{\mathrm{ii}} = 3\), in index notation \(\delta_{\mathrm{ii}} = 3\),
  3. for the unit vectors of the axes, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
Proof

We read all three items from the table in figure 2.128.

  1. Choose a value of the free index \(\ix{i}\). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\) has three terms. By definition 2.58, \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) in both terms in which \(\ix{j} \neq \ix{i}\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1\) in the term in which \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\). The sum is therefore \(1 \cdot a_{\mathrm{i}} = a_{\mathrm{i}}\). The same for a matrix, where the index \(\ix{k}\) stays fixed all along: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,A_{\mathrm{jk}} = 1 \cdot A_{\mathrm{ik}}\).
  2. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \delta_{\mathrm{ii}} = \delta_{\mathrm{xx}} + \delta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \delta_{\mathrm{zz}}\) has three diagonal elements, each is \(1\), so the sum is \(3\).
  3. By (1.12) and definition 2.8, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 = 1\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 = 0\), and the same for the other pairs: the product is \(1\) for equal indices, on the diagonal, and \(0\) for different ones, off it.

Source: SADD (1.3.2) (PDF p. 15), CM (2.2.47) (PDF p. 54).

Item 2 is the trap from the list above: in index notation \(\delta_{\mathrm{ii}}\) is not the element \(\delta_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\) but the sum of three ones, that is \(3\). Let us test the substitution rule on numbers too. For \((a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}}) = (4, -2, 7)\) and \(\ix{i} = z\) we get \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta_{\mathrm{zj}}\,a_{\mathrm{j}} = 0 \cdot 4 + 0 \cdot (-2) + 1 \cdot 7 = 7 = a_{\mathrm{z}}\). With the delta we write the equality above from the section on the determinant by components: \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tau_0\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\), in index notation \((\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tau_0\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\). In the lectures the identity matrix is also written \(\underline{\underline{\delta}}\) or \(\underline{\underline{I}}\).

A dictionary of equations. The table holds equations that the book already has, in both notations. The left form is the one in which the book derives them, the right form is shown by the button Index notation or found in the lectures.

equation written out index notation
Cauchy's formula (2.27) \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\)
equilibrium equations (2.38) \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\)
equations of motion (section 2.7.9) \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = \rho\,a_{\mathrm{i}}\) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ji},\mathrm{j}} + b_{\mathrm{i}} = \rho\,a_{\mathrm{i}}\)
rule for a tensor (2.64) \(\bar A_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\) \(\bar A_{\mathrm{kl}} = Q_{\mathrm{ki}}\,Q_{\mathrm{lj}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\)
small strain tensor (1.59) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \dfrac12\Big(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} + u_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{i}})\)
small rotation tensor (1.62) \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \dfrac12\Big(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\) \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} - u_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{i}})\)
Green-Lagrange tensor (lemma 1.119) \(E_{\mathrm{ij}} = \dfrac12\Big(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\Big)\) \(E_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} + u_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{i}}\,u_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{j}})\)
orthogonal matrix (2.52) \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{ik}}\,Q_{\mathrm{jk}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) \(Q_{\mathrm{ik}}\,Q_{\mathrm{jk}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\)

In every row let us count the indices, as we did in the figure 2.127. In the Green-Lagrange tensor \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) are free and stand in each of the three terms, so these are nine equations. The index \(\ix{k}\) stands only in the last term, twice there, so this term is a sum of three products. In Cauchy's formula and in the equilibrium equations the dummy index is the first index of the stress, because with us the first index tells the face (definition 2.27). CM has the indices swapped and writes \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) (CM (4.2.10), PDF p. 183). Since we know that the stress matrix is symmetric, this is the same.

Three equations that we shall meet later we state only so that a reader of the lectures recognises them. In section 2.11 we shall look for directions \(\vek n\) and numbers \(\lambda\) for which \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\), in index notation \((\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \lambda\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\). In section 2.12.4 we shall subtract from the stress the mean of its diagonal components, \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tfrac13\,\big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sigma_{\mathrm{kk}}\big)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), in index notation \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tfrac13\,\sigma_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In chapter 3 the relation between stress and strain with two constants of the material \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) will be written as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\big)\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), in index notation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In all three the delta sees to it that the number is added only to the diagonal components.

The permutation symbol. In index notation the scalar product has the form \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\,b_{\mathrm{i}}\). What about the vector product from definition 2.33? Its components are differences of products, for example \((\vek a\times\vek b)_{\mathrm{x}} = a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\). In the component \(x\) the other two letters appear, in the order \(y\), \(z\) with a plus and in the order \(z\), \(y\) with a minus. The components \(y\) and \(z\) we got by exchanging the letters round the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\). So we need a sign that tells the sign of an order of three letters.

Let us write the letters on a circle (figure 2.129). On the left circle we read in the direction of the arrows \(x \to y \to z \to x\). We may start at any letter and we get the three orders \(xyz\), \(yzx\), \(zxy\). To these we assign the value \(+1\). On the right circle we read in the opposite direction and get the other three orders \(xzy\), \(zyx\), \(yxz\), to which we assign the value \(-1\). Three different letters can be ordered in \(3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6\) ways, because we have three choices for the first place, two for the second and one for the third, so the two circles have covered them all. An order of three different letters is called a permutation (permutacija), from the Latin permutare, to exchange. The orders from the left circle are even permutations (sode permutacije), those from the right circle odd permutations (lihe permutacije). The names tell with how many exchanges of two letters we reach the order from \(xyz\): \(yxz\) with one, \(yzx\) with two, first \(xyz \to yxz\) and then \(yxz \to yzx\).

Definition 2.60 Permutation symbol (permutacijski simbol)

The permutation symbol (permutacijski simbol) is the \(27\) numbers \(\perm{ijk}\), where the indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\), \(\ix{k}\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The even orders are read by the left circle, the odd ones by the right:

\[\perm{ijk} = \begin{cases} +1 , & \text{if } \ix{ijk} \text{ is one of the orders } xyz,\ yzx,\ zxy \text{ (an even permutation)} , \\ -1 , & \text{if } \ix{ijk} \text{ is one of the orders } xzy,\ zyx,\ yxz \text{ (an odd permutation)} , \\ \phantom{+}0 , & \text{if at least two indices are equal} . \end{cases}\]

Source: SADD (1.3.3) (PDF p. 15), where the symbol is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), CM (2.2.50) (PDF p. 54) with the symbol \(e_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) and with the two circles in figure 2.2.10 (PDF p. 55).

Of the \(27\) numbers six differ from zero, three are \(+1\) and three \(-1\) (SADD, PDF p. 15). From the circles we read two properties that we shall use. The first: if we move the indices round the cycle, the value does not change, \(\perm{ijk} = \perm{jki} = \perm{kij}\), because on the same circle we only start at another letter. The second: if we exchange two indices, the sign reverses, \(\perm{jik} = -\perm{ijk}\), because an exchange of two letters reverses the direction of reading, for example \(xyz \to yxz\). With equal indices both sides are zero. Books also call it the alternating symbol (alternirajoči simbol), because it changes sign at an exchange (SADD, PDF p. 15), and the Levi-Civita symbol after the mathematician from section 2.9.7. We write \(\perm{ijk}\) as CM does, because with us \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the strain. In the lectures the symbol is \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{ijk}}\).

Let us see what the double sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \perm{ijk}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\,b_{\mathrm{k}}\) does (figure 2.130). For each value of \(\ix{i}\) there are nine terms, and each has its own table: the left table is for \(\ix{i} = x\), the middle one for \(\ix{i} = y\), the right one for \(\ix{i} = z\). The rows are the values of \(\ix{j}\), the columns the values of \(\ix{k}\), and a cell holds the value \(\perm{ijk}\) with the term it multiplies. Seven cells in each table hold a zero, because two of their indices are equal. What remains is one cell with \(+1\) and one cell with \(-1\), and below the tables is the sum of these two terms, which is exactly the component of the vector product.

Lemma 2.61 Vector product with the permutation symbol (vektorski produkt s permutacijskim simbolom)

Let the vectors be written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system and let the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). Then for any vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) and all indices

  1. \((\vek a\times\vek b)_{\mathrm{i}} =\) \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \perm{ijk}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\,b_{\mathrm{k}}\), in index notation \((\vek a\times\vek b)_{\mathrm{i}} = \perm{ijk}\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\,b_{\mathrm{k}}\),
  2. \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \perm{jki}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), in index notation \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{k}} = \perm{jki}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\).
Proof

We must show that the double sum gives the components from (2.39). It has nine terms, but the symbol makes most of them zero.

  1. Take \(\ix{i} = x\). By definition 2.60, \(\perm{xjk} \neq 0\) only when all three indices are different, that is for \((\ix{j}, \ix{k}) = (y, z)\) and \((z, y)\). The first order, \(xyz\), is on the left circle, the second, \(xzy\), on the right one. Of the nine terms two remain, \(\perm{xyz}\,a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} + \perm{xzy}\,a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} = a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\), which is the component \(x\) in (2.39).
  2. For \(\ix{i} = y\) there remain \((\ix{j}, \ix{k}) = (z, x)\) with the order \(yzx\) and the value \(+1\) and \((x, z)\) with the order \(yxz\) and the value \(-1\): \(a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\). For \(\ix{i} = z\) there remain \((x, y)\) with \(zxy\) and \(+1\) and \((y, x)\) with \(zyx\) and \(-1\): \(a_{\mathrm{x}} b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\). These are the components \(y\) and \(z\) in (2.39), and item 1 is proved.
  3. For item 2 we put \(\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek b = \vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) into item 1. The component \(\ix{m}\) of the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is, by item 3 of lemma 2.59, equal to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{m}} =\) \(\delta_{\mathrm{jm}}\). Therefore \((\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{m}} \sum_{\mathrm{n}} \perm{imn}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kn}}\). By the substitution rule (item 1 of the same lemma), used twice, this is \(\perm{ijk}\), and after a move round the cycle \(\perm{jki}\). The vector with the components \(\perm{jki}\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \perm{jki}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: CM (2.2.49), (2.2.52) (PDF pp. 54-55).

Item 2 says in one line item 6 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product and its consequences: \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \perm{xyz}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), in the direction of the arrows, and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \perm{yxz}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), against them. The lemma requires a right-handed system, because the definition of the vector product already requires it. A test on numbers: for \(\vek a = (1, 2, 3)\) and \(\vek b = (4, 5, 6)\) we get \((\vek a\times\vek b)_{\mathrm{x}} = \perm{xyz} \cdot 2 \cdot 6 + \perm{xzy} \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 12 - 15 = -3\), as (2.39) gives, \(a_{\mathrm{y}} b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}} b_{\mathrm{y}} = 2 \cdot 6 - 3 \cdot 5\).

When two permutation symbols meet in a calculation, we replace them by Kronecker deltas. In the lectures the two rules for this are left as homework, so let us prove them here.

Let us see what the rule says for one choice of indices (figure 2.131). On the left are the nine pairs \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\). On the diagonal the indices are equal, elsewhere different, and let us choose the pair \((x, y)\). On the right are the nine pairs \((\ix{m}, \ix{n})\), each with the value of the left side. The pair \((x, y)\) is the same as the chosen one and gives \(+1\), the pair \((y, x)\) is exchanged and gives \(-1\). The diagonal and the remaining four cells give \(0\).

Lemma 2.62 Product of two permutation symbols (produkt dveh permutacijskih simbolov)

Let the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) as in the tables. For all values of the free indices

  1. \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \perm{kij}\,\perm{kmn}\) \(= \delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jn}} - \delta_{\mathrm{in}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}}\), in index notation \(\perm{kij}\,\perm{kmn} = \delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jn}} - \delta_{\mathrm{in}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}}\),
  2. \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \perm{ijk}\,\perm{ijl} =\) \(2\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\), in index notation \(\perm{ijk}\,\perm{ijl} = 2\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\).
Proof

Item 1 has four free indices, so it is \(3^4 = 81\) equalities between numbers: nine pairs \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\), and for each nine pairs \((\ix{m}, \ix{n})\). We do not check them one by one but divide them into three groups. Item 2 we then get from item 1.

  1. The first group: \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\). The left side is zero, because \(\perm{kij}\) has two equal indices. The right side is \(\delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{in}} - \delta_{\mathrm{in}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{im}} = 0\). The same for \(\ix{m} = \ix{n}\): the left side is zero because of \(\perm{kmn}\), the right side is \(\delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}} - \delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}} = 0\).
  2. From here on let \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) and \(\ix{m} \neq \ix{n}\). The sum over \(\ix{k}\) has three terms. The symbol \(\perm{kij}\) is not zero only when \(\ix{k}\) is the third letter, different from \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\). On the circle, \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) are two of the three letters, \(\ix{k}\) is the remaining one. Of the three terms a single one therefore remains.
  3. The second group: the pair \((\ix{m}, \ix{n})\) has the same two letters as the pair \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\). If \((\ix{m}, \ix{n}) = (\ix{i}, \ix{j})\), the left side is \(\perm{kij}\,\perm{kij} = (\pm 1)^2 = 1\), and the right side \(\delta_{\mathrm{ii}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jj}} - \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ji}} = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 = 1\). Here \(\delta_{\mathrm{ii}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{jj}}\) mean one element each, without a sum. If \((\ix{m}, \ix{n}) = (\ix{j}, \ix{i})\), the left side is \(\perm{kij}\,\perm{kji} = -1\), because an exchange of two indices reverses the sign, and the right side \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ji}} - \delta_{\mathrm{ii}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jj}} = 0 - 1 = -1\).
  4. The third group: the pair \((\ix{m}, \ix{n})\) does not have the same two letters as \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\). Since \(\ix{m}\) and \(\ix{n}\) are different and are not exactly the letters \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), one of them is the third letter, that is \(\ix{k}\) from step 2. Then \(\perm{kmn}\) has two equal indices and the left side is zero. On the right, \(\delta_{\mathrm{im}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jn}}\) differs from zero only for \((\ix{m}, \ix{n}) = (\ix{i}, \ix{j})\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{in}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jm}}\) only for \((\ix{m}, \ix{n}) = (\ix{j}, \ix{i})\). Neither holds, so the right side is zero too. The groups cover all \(81\) choices, and item 1 is proved.
  5. Item 2. By a move round the cycle, \(\perm{ijk} = \perm{jki}\) and \(\perm{ijl} = \perm{jli}\). The sum over \(\ix{j}\) is, by item 1, in which the roles of the indices \(\ix{k}, \ix{i}, \ix{j}, \ix{m}, \ix{n}\) are taken by \(\ix{j}, \ix{k}, \ix{i}, \ix{l}, \ix{i}\), equal to
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \perm{jki}\,\perm{jli} = \delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ii}} - \delta_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}} ,\]
    where \(\delta_{\mathrm{ii}}\) is one element, that is \(1\).
  6. We sum over \(\ix{i}\) as well. The first term gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} \cdot (1 + 1 + 1) = 3\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\). In the second, by the substitution rule (item 1 of lemma 2.59), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \delta_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}} = \delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\). The difference is \(3\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} - \delta_{\mathrm{kl}} = 2\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\).

Source: CM (2.2.55) (PDF p. 55). SADD writes a more general relation with a determinant (SADD (1.3.5), PDF p. 15).

The proof showed that the product of two symbols with a common first index only compares the pairs of the remaining indices: \(+1\) if the pairs are equal, \(-1\) if they are exchanged, and \(0\) otherwise. All \(81\) equalities of item 1 and the nine equalities of item 2 we also checked with SymPy, by computing the sums for all values of the indices. Where does the two in item 2 come from? For \(\ix{k} = \ix{l} = z\) two terms of the double sum differ from zero, \((\ix{i}, \ix{j}) = (x, y)\) and \((y, x)\), one from each circle, each with the square \((\pm 1)^2 = 1\).

The order of a tensor and the number of components. A symbol with one index, \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\), is three numbers, with two, \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), nine, with three, \(\perm{ijk}\), twenty-seven. Every index has three values, so a symbol with \(r\) indices has \(3^r\) numbers (SADD, PDF p. 12). In the plane, where the indices run only over \(x\) and \(y\), there are \(2^r\), and in general \(d^r\), where \(d\) is the number of axes.

In figure 2.132 every component is one small square. The column of three is a vector, a first-order tensor from definition 2.56. The three by three table is a second-order tensor, for example the stress. Every new index triples the whole picture: three tables are a quantity with three indices, one table for each value of the third index, and nine tables a quantity with four indices. The numbers below them are \(3\), \(9\), \(27\) and \(81\). A quantity with four indices whose components change, when the axes are turned, by the rule with four factors \(Q\), one for each index, is a fourth-order tensor (tenzor četrtega reda) (SADD (1.5.1), PDF p. 18). Such a tensor with \(81\) components will, in chapter 3, connect the nine components of the stress with the nine components of the strain (SADD, PDF p. 91). The number of indices alone does not make a tensor: what decides is the rule when the axes are turned, as in definition 2.56.

2.9.9 The curl and the axial vector of the rotation

Section 1.17.5 left open how the rotations in the three coordinate planes combine into a single rotation about one axis. There we found that the antisymmetric part of the displacement gradient, the small rotation tensor \(\ten\omega\) (definition 1.122), turns a short fibre \(\vek z\) from the point \(P\) through a small angle without changing its length, up to terms with squares of the derivatives. The matrix \(\ten\omega\) has only three different numbers, and for a small rotation of the body about the axis \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\) by the angle \(\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\) or \(\theta_{\mathrm{z}}\) these were \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \theta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\theta_{\mathrm{z}}\). Three numbers are exactly as many as a vector has. To combine them we needed a calculation that from two vectors gives a third, perpendicular to both. Now we have it, it is the vector product, and with it we will write the displacement of the tip.

Let us draw what we are looking for (figure 2.133). From the point \(O\), which is the end of the fibre at the point \(P\), we draw the fibre \(\vek z\) before the rotation. Through \(O\) goes the axis about which the material near the point turns. The tip of the fibre moves along a circle about the axis, of radius \(\rho\), and the fibre comes into its position after the rotation. The difference is the displacement of the tip. For a small angle the displacement is almost straight, perpendicular to the axis and to the fibre, and its length is the angle times the radius \(\rho\). Perpendicular to two vectors is their vector product. So let us try to describe the rotation by one vector \(\vek\omega\) along the axis, whose length is the angle of rotation in radians, and to write the displacement as \(\vek\omega\times\vek z\). The curved arrow shows the sense of turning: if the thumb of the right hand points along \(\vek\omega\), the fingers show which way the material turns.

Definition 2.63 Axial vector of the small rotation (osni vektor malega zasuka)

Let \(\ten\omega\) be the small rotation tensor at an interior point \(P\) of the body, written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system. The axial vector (osni vektor) of the small rotation at the point \(P\) is the vector along the axis of rotation

\[\vek\omega = (\omega_{\mathrm{x}},\ \omega_{\mathrm{y}},\ \omega_{\mathrm{z}}) = (-\omega_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \ \omega_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \ -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}) . \tag{2.65}\]

Source: CM (3.5.13), (3.5.14) (PDF p. 143), SADD (2.1.9) (PDF p. 41), where it is called the dual vector (dualni vektor).

Let us draw what equation (2.65) connects (figure 2.134). On the left is the matrix \(\ten\omega\), on the right the vector \(\vek\omega\). The diagonal is zero, because the matrix is antisymmetric. Above the diagonal are \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), each with an arrow to one component of the vector and with the sign given by (2.65). The elements below the diagonal are the same three with the opposite sign, so we do not count them separately.

The components of a vector have one index, the elements of a tensor two, so we tell them apart although they carry the same letter: \(\omega_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a component of the vector, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) an element of the matrix. By section 1.17.5 the components of the axial vector are exactly the angles \(\omega_{\mathrm{x}} = \theta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{y}} = \theta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{z}} = \theta_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the rotations about the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). In the lectures the small rotation tensor is \(\underline{\underline{\Omega}}\), the linear rotation tensor, and the axial vector is \(\vec\omega\).

Lemma 2.64 The small rotation tensor as a vector product (tenzor malih zasukov kot vektorski produkt)

Let \(\ten\omega\) be the small rotation tensor and \(\vek\omega\) its axial vector at an interior point \(P\) of the body, in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and let the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). Then:

  1. for every vector \(\vek z\), \(\ten\omega\,\vek z = \vek\omega\times\vek z\),
  2. \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \perm{ijk}\,\omega_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = -\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \perm{ijk}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\), in index notation \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = -\perm{ijk}\,\omega_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = -\tfrac12\,\perm{ijk}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
Proof

Item 1 we show by components, item 2 with lemma 2.62.

  1. By definition 1.122 the matrix \(\ten\omega\) has the rows \((0,\ \omega_{\mathrm{xy}},\ \omega_{\mathrm{xz}})\), \((-\omega_{\mathrm{xy}},\ 0,\ \omega_{\mathrm{yz}})\) and \((-\omega_{\mathrm{xz}},\ -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}},\ 0)\). Into them we put (2.65), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \omega_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{x}}\). By (1.39),
    \[\ten\omega\,\vek z = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_{\mathrm{z}} & \omega_{\mathrm{y}} \\ \omega_{\mathrm{z}} & 0 & -\omega_{\mathrm{x}} \\ -\omega_{\mathrm{y}} & \omega_{\mathrm{x}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} z_{\mathrm{x}} \\ z_{\mathrm{y}} \\ z_{\mathrm{z}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_{\mathrm{y}} z_{\mathrm{z}} - \omega_{\mathrm{z}} z_{\mathrm{y}} \\ \omega_{\mathrm{z}} z_{\mathrm{x}} - \omega_{\mathrm{x}} z_{\mathrm{z}} \\ \omega_{\mathrm{x}} z_{\mathrm{y}} - \omega_{\mathrm{y}} z_{\mathrm{x}} \end{bmatrix} .\]
  2. By (2.39), with \(\vek a = \vek\omega\) and \(\vek b = \vek z\), these are the components of the vector \(\vek\omega\times\vek z\), the displacement of the tip in figure 2.133. Item 1 is proved.
  3. The first equality of item 2. For \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) both sides are zero, like the diagonal. For \((\ix{i}, \ix{j}) = (x, y)\) the term with \(\ix{k} = z\) remains in the sum: \(-\perm{xyz}\,\omega_{\mathrm{z}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{z}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\). For \((x, z)\) there remains \(\ix{k} = y\): \(-\perm{xzy}\,\omega_{\mathrm{y}} = \omega_{\mathrm{y}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\). For \((y, z)\) there remains \(\ix{k} = x\): \(-\perm{yzx}\,\omega_{\mathrm{x}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{x}} = \omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\). When we exchange the indices, both sides change sign, the left one by definition 1.122, the right one because of the permutation symbol, as for the elements below the diagonal.
  4. The second equality. We multiply the first by \(\perm{ijl}\) and sum over \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\). By item 2 of lemma 2.62 and by the substitution rule,
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \perm{ijl}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \perm{ijl}\,\perm{ijk}\Big)\,\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}} 2\,\delta_{\mathrm{lk}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = -2\,\omega_{\mathrm{l}} .\]
    We divide by \(-2\) and rename the index \(\ix{l}\) to \(\ix{k}\).

Source: CM (3.5.14) and the line below (3.5.15) (PDF p. 143).

The lemma says that the displacement of the tip of the fibre due to the rotation really is a vector product, as we guessed from the figure. Now we read everything the figure shows from the properties of the vector product.

  • The axis. For a fibre along the axial vector, \(\vek z = s\,\vek\omega\), items 1 and 3 of lemma 2.34 give \(\vek\omega\times(s\,\vek\omega) = s\,(\vek\omega\times\vek\omega) = \vek 0\). The points on the line through \(O\) in the direction of \(\vek\omega\) do not move, and this is the axis of rotation.
  • The direction of the displacement. By item 4 of the same lemma \(\vek\omega\times\vek z\) is perpendicular to \(\vek\omega\) and to \(\vek z\), so it is tangent to the circle about the axis.
  • The size. By item 5, \(|\vek\omega\times\vek z|^2 = |\vek\omega|^2\,|\vek z|^2 - (\vek\omega\cdot\vek z)^2\). Let \(\vek z_\parallel\) be the projection of the fibre on the axis and \(\rho\) the distance of the tip from the axis. Then \((\vek\omega\cdot\vek z)^2 = |\vek\omega|^2\,|\vek z_\parallel|^2\) and by the Pythagorean theorem \(|\vek z|^2 = |\vek z_\parallel|^2 + \rho^2\), so \(|\vek\omega\times\vek z| = |\vek\omega|\,\rho\). The displacement is the angle times the radius, like the length of an arc, and the angle of rotation is \(|\vek\omega|\) radians.

The three rotations in the three planes are thus the three components of one arrow. Let us test it on numbers. At some point let \(\vek\omega = (1,\ 2,\ 2)\) mrad, that is \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = -1\) mrad, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\) mrad and \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -2\) mrad. The length is \(|\vek\omega| = 1\ \text{mrad} \cdot \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3\) mrad, which is \(0{,}17^\circ\), and the axis points in the direction \((1, 2, 2)/3\). For the fibre \(\vek z = (20,\ 10,\ 0)\) mm,

\[\vek\omega\times\vek z = (2 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 10,\ \ 2 \cdot 20 - 1 \cdot 0,\ \ 1 \cdot 10 - 2 \cdot 20)\ \text{mrad}\cdot\text{mm} = (-20,\ 40,\ -30)\ \text{µm} .\]

The displacement is \(\sqrt{20^2 + 40^2 + 30^2}\) µm \(= 53{,}9\) µm long. The distance of the tip from the axis is \(\rho = 17{,}95\) mm, and \(0{,}003 \cdot 17{,}95\) mm \(= 53{,}9\) µm (computed with SymPy). The displacement is perpendicular to the fibre, \((-20) \cdot 20 + 40 \cdot 10 + (-30) \cdot 0 = 0\).

Where does the assumption of a small rotation enter here? A true rotation moves the tip along an arc of the circle, while \(\vek\omega\times\vek z\) is a straight line, tangent to it. By section 1.17.5 the end of the straight line lies about \(\tfrac12\,|\vek\omega|^2\rho\) outside the circle. In the example this is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}003^2 \cdot 17{,}95\) mm \(= 8 \cdot 10^{-5}\) mm, almost seven hundred times less than the displacement. At the angle \(0{,}3\) rad the error would already be \(15\) percent of the displacement, and the description with \(\ten\omega\) then does not hold (section 1.17.6). For the same reason we may add small rotations as vectors, but not large ones: the sum \(\vek\omega\times\vek z + \vek\omega'\times\vek z = (\vek\omega + \vek\omega')\times\vek z\), by item 2 of lemma 2.34, holds for the straight lines, not for the arcs.

Let us look at the plane \(xy\) near the point \(P\) (figure 2.135). On the left the body turns as a whole. The fibre along \(x\) tilts by the angle \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\). The fibre along \(y\) tilts in the same sense, by the angle \(-\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\), since its tip slips in the negative direction of \(x\). The rotation about the axis \(z\) is the mean of the two angles. On the right is a stretch along \(x\): the fibres keep their directions, both angles are zero.

The curl. We compute the axial vector directly from the displacement field, for \(\omega_{\mathrm{z}}\) from the two tilts of the fibres. By definitions 2.63 and 1.122,

\[\omega_{\mathrm{x}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}\Big) , \quad \omega_{\mathrm{y}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \quad \omega_{\mathrm{z}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) .\]

The differences of derivatives in the brackets have the same pattern as the components of the vector product in (2.39), only that in the place of the components of the first vector stand the derivatives with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The vector of these three differences has its own name.

Definition 2.65 Curl of a vector field (rotor vektorskega polja)

Let the vector field \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\), written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, have all partial derivatives of the first order at the point \(P\). The curl (rotor) of the field \(\vek v\) at the point \(P\) is the vector of differences of derivatives

\[\operatorname{rot}\vek v = \Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z},\ \ \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x},\ \ \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) , \tag{2.66}\]
\[(\operatorname{rot}\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} = \perm{ijk}\,v_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{j}} , \tag{2.66}\]

with all derivatives at the point \(P\), for the component \(z\) these are the tilts of the fibres.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.9 (1) (PDF p. 432), SADD (1.8.4) (PDF p. 26). Both also write \(\nabla\times\vek v\), KREYSZIG also \(\operatorname{curl}\vek v\).

The Slovenian name rotor and the sign rot come from rotation: KREYSZIG explains the notation rot exactly by the rotation of a rigid body (KREYSZIG §9.9, PDF p. 433). The index form follows from item 1 of lemma 2.61, if we put the derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the place of \(a_{\mathrm{j}}\). By comparing the three differences above with (2.66) we get

\[\vek\omega = \tfrac12\,\operatorname{rot}\vek u . \tag{2.67}\]

This relation is written by CM (3.5.15) (PDF p. 143) and SADD (PDF p. 41). Where does the half come from? For a rotation of the body as a whole about the axis \(z\) by a small angle \(\theta\), with the displacement \(\vek u \approx (-\theta\,y,\ \theta\,x,\ 0)\) from section 1.17.5, we get \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x - \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = \theta - (-\theta) = 2\theta\). Both derivatives tell the same angle, one by the tilt of the fibre along \(x\), the other by the tilt of the fibre along \(y\), the curl adds them, so we halve it. The result is \(\vek\omega = (0, 0, \theta)\), an arrow along the axis \(z\), as it must be.

Three examples show what the curl measures and what it does not.

  • A rotation of the body as a whole, just now: \(\operatorname{rot}\vek u = (0, 0, 2\theta)\), the strains are zero. Every fibre turns by the same angle, as in the figure.
  • A stretch along one axis, \(\vek u = (a\,x,\ 0,\ 0)\): all derivatives in (2.66) are zero, so \(\operatorname{rot}\vek u = \vek 0\). The material deforms, but it turns at no point.
  • The sheared cube from section 1.6.2, \(\vek u = (10^{-3}\,z,\ 0,\ 0)\): the only derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = 0{,}001\), so \(\operatorname{rot}\vek u = (0,\ 10^{-3},\ 0)\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}0005\) rad. The cube as a whole does not rotate, since its bottom face stays on the table, yet the axial vector is not zero. The reason is that the vertical edges get the tilt \(0{,}001\), while the horizontal ones get no tilt. The rotation tensor takes the mean of the two, \(0{,}0005\), and the other half of the shift is described by the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\). So the axial vector does not say that the body rotates, but by how much the fibres at the point turn on average.

2.9.10 Compatibility with the curl

In chapter 1 we got the compatibility equations (theorem 1.133) from three displacements that give six strains: six functions cannot be arbitrary if they are to come from three. In the lectures the same equations are derived in four lines with the curl, which we draw below as a scheme, and written as a single line, \(\nabla\times(\nabla\times\ten\varepsilon)^\T = \mat 0\). This section is a bridge between the two notations: it shows what the line means by components and that it is the six equations of the theorem. The proofs of the book stay as they are. Two relations that the lectures use without proof we prove here.

The idea is a single one and we already know it. If we differentiate a function with respect to \(x\) and then with respect to \(y\), we get the same as in the reverse order (theorem 1.131). Therefore the three partial derivatives of one function are not three arbitrary functions. In section 1.18.3 we saw this on a small rectangle: when we go round it and add up the changes of the function, we must return to the same value. The curl is the calculation that checks this at a point.

We look at the same idea in space, for the second item of the lemma (figure 2.136).

Let us draw a small cube near the point \(P\). The curl tells how much the field circulates around each face, that is along its four edges. The circulation around the front face and around the right face pass the common edge in opposite directions, so their contributions on it cancel. The same holds at all twelve edges, and the sum of the circulations over all six faces is zero.

Lemma 2.66 The curl of a field of partial derivatives is zero (rotor polja parcialnih odvodov je nič)

Let the function \(f\) of three variables have, at every point of an open set \(D\), partial derivatives of the first and second order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Then:

  1. for the field of its partial derivatives \(\vek g = (\partial f/\partial x,\ \partial f/\partial y,\ \partial f/\partial z)\), at every point of \(D\), \(\operatorname{rot}\vek g = \vek 0\),
  2. if a vector field \(\vek v\) has, at every point of \(D\), partial derivatives of the first and second order that are continuous at every point of \(D\), then at every point of \(D\) the sum \(\partial(\operatorname{rot}\vek v)_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial(\operatorname{rot}\vek v)_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial(\operatorname{rot}\vek v)_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\).
Proof

Both items are the symmetry of mixed derivatives, written with the curl: the first on the rectangle, the second on the cube.

  1. The component \(z\) of the curl of the field \(\vek g\) is, by (2.66), \(\partial g_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x - \partial g_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\), that is the difference of the mixed derivatives of the function \(f\), once first with respect to \(y\) and then \(x\), once the other way round. By theorem 1.131 on the symmetry of mixed derivatives they are equal, like the changes along the two paths round the rectangle, so the difference is zero. The components \(x\) and \(y\) are differences of mixed derivatives with respect to \(y\), \(z\) and to \(z\), \(x\), and are zero for the same reason.
  2. Item 2. By (2.66) the sum equals
    \[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}\Big) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) .\]
    Every component appears twice, with opposite signs and with the derivatives in exchanged order, for example \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the first and in the fourth term. By theorem 1.131 the terms cancel in pairs.

Source: SADD (1.8.5) (PDF p. 26), where the two relations are listed among the identities.

We imagine the matrix as three columns, each of which is a vector field. We take the curl of each column separately, and the three vectors we get are the columns of the new matrix.

The curl of a matrix we take by columns. For a matrix field \(\mat A\) let \(\operatorname{rot}\mat A\) be the matrix whose column \(\ix{j}\) is the curl of the vector field from the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\mat A\):

\[(\operatorname{rot}\mat A)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \perm{lki}\,\frac{\partial A_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} . \tag{2.68}\]
\[(\operatorname{rot}\mat A)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \perm{lki}\,A_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{k}} . \tag{2.68}\]

This is what the lectures write \(\nabla\times\mat A\). Now we read the four lines of the lectures as four steps on a scheme (figure 2.138).

Lemma 2.67 Compatibility equations with the curl (enačbe kompatibilnosti z rotorjem)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, and let the components of the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) have, at every point of \(D\), partial derivatives of the first, second and third order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient, \(\ten\varepsilon\) the small strain tensor, \(\ten\omega\) the small rotation tensor and \(\vek\omega\) its axial vector, in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and let the curl of a matrix be taken by columns ((2.68)). Then at every point of \(D\):

  1. \(\operatorname{rot}\mat H^\T = \mat 0\),
  2. \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) for all \(\ix{l}\) and \(\ix{j}\), which is nine of the equalities (1.77),
  3. \(\operatorname{rot}\big((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)^\T\big) = \mat 0\), and these nine equalities are the six compatibility equations (1.76), three of them written twice.
Proof

We go along the scheme in figure 2.138 from left to right, first along the top row, then along the bottom one.

  1. The top row. The element of the matrix \(\mat H^\T\) in the row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) is \(H_{\mathrm{ji}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) (definitions 1.112 and 1.101). The column \(\ix{j}\) is therefore \((\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x,\ \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial y,\ \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial z)\), the field of partial derivatives of one function, the component \(u_{\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 2.66 its curl is zero, and this holds for all three columns. This is item 1.
  2. The split. By section 1.17.5, \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\). We transpose: \(\ten\varepsilon\) is symmetric, \(\ten\omega\) antisymmetric, so \(\mat H^\T = \ten\varepsilon - \ten\omega\). The curl by columns is a difference of derivatives, so the curl of a difference is the difference of the curls (lemma 1.82), and from item 1 it follows that \(\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon = \operatorname{rot}\ten\omega\).
  3. The curl of the rotation tensor. By item 2 of lemma 2.64, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{m}} \perm{ijm}\,\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\). We put this into (2.68):
    \[(\operatorname{rot}\ten\omega)_{\mathrm{lj}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{m}} \perm{lki}\,\perm{ijm}\,\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{m}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{m}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \perm{ilk}\,\perm{ijm}\Big)\,\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{m}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} ,\]
    where we moved the indices of the first symbol round the cycle, \(\perm{lki} = \perm{ilk}\).
  4. By item 1 of lemma 2.62, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \perm{ilk}\,\perm{ijm} = \delta_{\mathrm{lj}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{km}} - \delta_{\mathrm{lm}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kj}}\).
