By the substitution rule (lemma 2.59) the first term gives \(-\delta_{\mathrm{lj}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\omega_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\), and the second \(+\partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\):
    \[(\operatorname{rot}\ten\omega)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \delta_{\mathrm{lj}}\,\Big(\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big) .\]
  5. The bracket is zero. By (2.67), \(\vek\omega = \tfrac12\,\operatorname{rot}\vek u\), and by item 2 of lemma 2.66 the sum in the bracket is zero for the curl of any field. With step 2, \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  6. The comparison with (1.77). Take \(\ix{l} = z\) and \(\ix{j} = x\). By (2.66) the left side is \(\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y\) and the right side \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = -\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial x\). The equality (1.77) with \((\ix{i}, \ix{j}, \ix{k}) = (x, y, x)\) says \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial x = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x\), the same. The other eight pairs likewise.
  7. The bottom row, the last step. The matrix \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)^\T\) has in the row \(\ix{j}\) and column \(\ix{l}\) the element \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). Its column \(\ix{l}\) is \((\partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x,\ \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial y,\ \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial z)\), again the field of partial derivatives of one function, now the component \(\omega_{\mathrm{l}}\). This has continuous second derivatives, because \(\vek u\) has continuous third ones. By lemma 2.66 the curl of every column is zero, as in the top row.
  8. Element \(zz\) of \(\mat S = \operatorname{rot}\big((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)^\T\big)\). The column \(z\) of \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)^\T\) has the components \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)_{\mathrm{zx}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y\) and \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)_{\mathrm{zy}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial x - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y\). The component \(z\) of its curl is
    \[S_{\mathrm{zz}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} .\]
    By symmetry of \(\ten\varepsilon\) and of mixed derivatives, \(S_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) is the first equation of (1.76).
  9. In the same way \(S_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) is equation (2) and \(S_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) equation (3). Off the diagonal \(\mat S\) is symmetric, and \(S_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), \(S_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), \(S_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) are equations (4), (5), (6), each multiplied by \(-1\). SymPy compared all nine elements with the six equations.

Source: The proof is ours, put together from lemma 1.134 (SADD (2.6.6), PDF p. 52) and lemma 2.66. The six equations themselves: CM (3.7.4)-(3.7.9) (PDF p. 151), SADD (2.6.2) (PDF p. 51).

What did the lemma show? The compatibility equations say two things at once, as the two rows of the scheme show. The columns of the matrix \(\mat H^\T\) are derivatives of the displacements, so their curl is zero, and from this follows how the axial vector changes from point to point: its derivatives are determined by the derivatives of the strains. These derivatives, in turn, are derivatives of the three functions \(\omega_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{z}}\), so their curl must be zero too. We took the curl twice, and this is why the equations hold second derivatives of the strains. The assumption of continuous third derivatives of the displacements we used in step 7, as in the proof of theorem 1.133. Without it the mixed derivatives need not be equal, and lemma 2.66 does not hold.

Now let us read the lines of the lectures. The sign \(\nabla\vek u\) is there the matrix with the element \(\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\), that is our \(\mat H^\T\). The sign \(\underline{\underline{I}}\times\vec\omega\) is the matrix with the elements \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \perm{ikj}\,\omega_{\mathrm{k}}\), which by item 2 of lemma 2.64 is our \(\ten\omega\). The lines thus match the steps of the proof:

in the lectures in the book where
\(\nabla\vek u = \ten\varepsilon - \underline{\underline{I}}\times\vec\omega\) \(\mat H^\T = \ten\varepsilon - \ten\omega\) step 2
\(\underline{\underline{I}}\times(\nabla\times\vek a) = (\nabla\vek a)^\T - \nabla\vek a\), without proof \(\ten\omega = \tfrac12\,(\mat H - \mat H^\T)\) with \(\vek\omega = \tfrac12\,\operatorname{rot}\vek u\) lemma 2.64 and (2.67)
\(\nabla\times(\nabla\vek u) = \mat 0\) \(\operatorname{rot}\mat H^\T = \mat 0\) item 1
\(\nabla\times(\underline{\underline{I}}\times\vek a) = (\nabla\vek a)^\T - \underline{\underline{I}}\,\nabla\cdot\vek a\), without proof \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\omega)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \delta_{\mathrm{lj}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial\omega_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) steps 3 and 4
\(\nabla\times\ten\varepsilon = (\nabla\vec\omega)^\T\) \((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)_{\mathrm{lj}} = \partial\omega_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) item 2
\(\nabla\times(\nabla\times\ten\varepsilon)^\T = \mat 0\) \(\operatorname{rot}\big((\operatorname{rot}\ten\varepsilon)^\T\big) = \mat 0\) item 3
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{km}}\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{kil}}\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{mjn}} = 0\) \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{m}} \perm{kil}\,\perm{mjn}\,\dfrac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{m}}} = 0\) element \(S_{\mathrm{nl}}\), steps 8 and 9

In the second and fourth rows \(\vek a\) is an arbitrary vector field, and steps 3 and 4 and lemma 2.64 hold for every field, not only for \(\vek u\) and \(\vek\omega\), because they use only the definitions. In the last row \(\ix{n}\) and \(\ix{l}\) are free, so these are nine equations, the other four indices are dummies, and every equation is a sum of \(81\) terms, of which the two permutation symbols leave at most four, as in step 8. Let us test it on an example that does not satisfy the equations: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\,y^2\), all other components zero. Then \(S_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y^2 = 2c\), which is not zero. No displacement field gives such strains, as the first equation of (1.76) already says. The field \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\,y\), however, gives \(S_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), and for it a displacement exists, for example \(\vek u = (c\,x\,y,\ -\tfrac12\,c\,x^2,\ 0)\), where \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = c\,y\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = c\,x - c\,x = 0\).

Let us return to the stress and to the two questions from the beginning of section 2.9.

In pure shear we found axes in which all shear components of the stress are zero, and for the sheared cube axes in which all shear components of the strain are zero. In the axes of pure shear, along the diagonals of the cube, the normal stress was \(\tau_0\) on one face and \(-\tau_0\) on another. Do such axes exist for every stress? And is \(\tau_0\) the largest normal stress on all faces through the point? This is the second question from the beginning of the section. On a face perpendicular to such an axis the traction vector is parallel to the normal. Whether such a direction exists is decided by a single number that we compute from the matrix, and this number is the subject of section 2.10.
